sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces slope stability analysis as a core geotechnical engineering discipline, emphasizing that it combines statics, soil/rock mechanics, and numerical methods. Notes that solution methods range from simple chart solutions to complex computer analyses, and that shear strength is the most critical parameter. Distinguishes rock slope stability from soil slope stability, noting different failure modes.
sections.body:
Slope stability analysis is a common category of analyses in geotechnical engineering practice. The analysis contains elements of statics, rock or soil mechanics, and numerical methods. The techniques used range from simple chart solutions to complicated numerical computer solutions. Regardless of the solution method employed, the most important element in slope stability analysis is the shear strength of the soil or rock.

Although rock slope stability and soil slope stability rely on the same basic mechanics, the modes of failure can be very different. In this chapter, rock slope stability will be discussed in a separate stand-alone section.
key_points: Slope stability analysis integrates statics, rock/soil mechanics, and numerical methods.
Solution techniques span from simple chart solutions to complex numerical computer methods.
Regardless of the solution method, the most important element in slope stability analysis is the shear strength of the soil or rock.
Rock and soil slope stability rely on the same basic mechanics, but the modes of failure can be very different.
Rock slope stability is treated in a separate stand-alone section within the chapter.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever slope stability analysis is being conducted for any soil or rock slope in geotechnical engineering practice.

sections.title: Types of Slopes and Modes of Failure
sections.summary: Classifies slopes into natural slopes, cuts (cut or excavated slopes) and embankments of compacted soil (highway embankments, dams and levees, fill slopes, MSE slopes). Gives the principal modes of failure (rotation on a curved slip surface approximated by a circular arc, translation on a planar surface, displacement of a wedge along planes of weakness) and other modes such as toppling, falls, block slides, lateral spreading, earth and mud flow, and debris flows. Figures 7-1 and 7-2 show failure conditions for natural slopes and for embankment foundations and cut slopes.
sections.body:
There are many different categories of slopes. Natural slopes are those that are ungraded and the slope geometry is controlled by nature. Figure 7-1 shows some general cross-sections and failure conditions for natural slopes. If the slope is steepened by grading or excavation, it is called a cut, a cut slope or an excavated slope. Dam abutments can be natural slopes or cut slopes.

Embankments constructed of compacted soil form another category of slopes. These embankments can be highway embankments, dams and levees, fill slopes, Mechanically Stabilized Earth (MSE) slopes, and others. Figure 7-2 shows cross-sections through example embankment slopes and details about the failure conditions.

Principal modes of failure in soil or rock are (i) rotation on a curved slip surface approximated by a circular arc, (ii) translation on a planar surface whose length is large compared to depth below ground, and (iii) displacement of a wedge-shaped mass along one or more planes of weakness. Other modes of failure include toppling of rock slopes, falls, block slides, lateral spreading, earth and mud flow in clayey and silty soils, and debris flows in coarse-grained soils. Figure 7-1 and 7-2 show examples of potential slope failure problems in both natural and man-made slopes.
key_points: Slopes are categorized as natural (ungraded), cut/excavated, or compacted embankments (dams, levees, MSE slopes, highway fills).
Three principal failure modes: (1) rotational failure on a circular arc slip surface, (2) translational failure on a planar surface, (3) wedge displacement along planes of weakness.
Other modes of failure include toppling of rock slopes, falls, block slides, lateral spreading, earth and mud flow in clayey and silty soils, and debris flows in coarse-grained soils.
Dam abutments may be classified as either natural slopes or cut slopes.
Figures 7-1 and 7-2 illustrate typical failure conditions for natural slopes and embankment/cut slopes, respectively.

sections.applicability: Applies when identifying the slope category and anticipated failure mode for any natural slope, cut slope, or compacted embankment being evaluated for stability.

sections.title: Definition of Factor of Safety
sections.summary: Defines the factor of safety (F) for slope stability as the ratio of shear strength (s) to shear stress required for equilibrium (τ), per Eq. 7-1. Explains stability conditions relative to F=1, and notes that the shear strength s depends on the strength model, soil type, and drainage conditions. References Table 7-1 for applicable strength models.
sections.body:
The stability of slopes is characterized by the factor of safety, F. Although there have been various methods of defining the factor of safety found in the engineering literature, the most common is shown below:

F = s/τ  (7-1)

where:
s = shear strength,
τ = shear stress required for equilibrium.

If the factor of safety is equal to unity, the slope is in a condition of barely stable equilibrium, right at the point of failure. As the factor of safety increases above unity, the stability of the slope increases. Slopes having a factor of safety less than one are considered unstable.

The value of s used in the calculation of factor of safety depends on the strength model used to characterize the soil, which is often associated with the drainage conditions assumed as well as the soil type. Table 7-1 shows different strength models that can be used in the analyses for different soil types and drainage conditions. [Note to Table 7-1: σʹff = effective stress on failure plane, φʹ = effective stress friction angle, cʹ = effective cohesion, σff = total normal stress on failure plane, φ = total stress friction angle, c = total stress cohesion, ssu = undrained steady state shear strength, and su = undrained shear strength]

The shear stress required for equilibrium (τ) is calculated by statics along with assumptions regarding the conditions for equilibrium and other factors. The number of unknowns exceeds the number of equilibrium equations in most forms of slope stability analysis, so assumptions must be made. A major difference in the various methods used to perform slope stability analyses is the conditions of equilibrium that are satisfied.
key_points: Factor of safety F = s/τ, where s is shear strength and τ is shear stress required for equilibrium (Eq. 7-1).
F = 1 indicates barely stable equilibrium (onset of failure); F < 1 indicates instability.
The shear strength s depends on the strength model, soil type, and assumed drainage conditions.
Unknowns exceed equilibrium equations in most slope stability analyses, requiring assumptions.
Table 7-1 provides strength models for various soil types and drainage conditions.

sections.title: Methods of Analysis of Soil Slopes
sections.summary: Introduces the three principal numerical procedures used to assess slope stability: limit equilibrium analysis, finite element/finite difference analysis, and plasticity (limit) analysis. Provides historical context for development of quantitative slope stability methods beginning in the 1920s and notes varying degrees of practical popularity for each approach.
sections.body:
Slope stability analysis in geotechnical engineering practice has evolved over the past 100 years. Initial methods of assessing the stability of slopes involved mapping areas of instability and determining slope angles from surveys to create landslide hazard maps. These types of maps are still produced and can be useful in screening potential stability issues with natural slopes and examining regional landslide risk. Beginning in the 1920s, assessment procedures were developed that provided a more quantitative basis for determining the stability of slopes.

Three numerical procedures are used, with varying degrees of popularity, to assess the stability of slopes: (1) limit equilibrium analysis, (2) finite element and finite difference analysis, and (3) plasticity analysis.
key_points: Three main numerical methods for slope stability: limit equilibrium, finite element/finite difference, and plasticity (limit) analysis.
Landslide hazard maps based on slope mapping remain useful for screening natural slopes and regional risk.
Quantitative slope stability assessment methods have been in development since the 1920s.
The three procedures are used with varying degrees of popularity.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting an appropriate numerical method to assess the stability of soil slopes in geotechnical engineering practice.

sections.title: Limit Equilibrium Analysis
sections.summary: Describes limit equilibrium analysis, the most popular method for soil slopes: the sliding mass is divided into free bodies, force and/or moment equilibrium gives the shear stress required for barely stable equilibrium, and Eq. 7-1 gives F. Failure surfaces can be linear, circular or combined; assumptions and, in many cases, iteration by computer are needed. Methods satisfying all equilibrium conditions (Spencer; Morgenstern and Price) give the most accurate answers. Covers searching for the critical surface and Bishop's Simplified Method (Figure 7-4).
sections.body:
Limit Equilibrium Analysis is the most popular method of analysis to quantify the stability of soil slopes. The procedure involves dividing the sliding mass into one or more free bodies, and determining the forces acting on the free bodies using equations for force and/or moment equilibrium. The shear stress required for a condition of barely-stable equilibrium (τ) is determined for each free body from the analysis of the system of free bodies. These shear stresses are used with Equation 7-1 to calculate the factor of safety of the slope.

Figure 7-3 shows the division of slopes into one, three, and multiple free bodies for analysis using the limit equilibrium method. For these analyses, the failure surface can be linear, circular, or a combination of linear and arc segments. For most limit equilibrium analyses, assumptions must be made so that the equilibrium equations can be satisfied. In many cases, iteration must be performed to obtain a solution, and it takes a computer program to efficiently apply the analysis method.

In general, the most common methods used in practice assume that the failure surface is circular or a surface comprised of many line segments. The methods that solve for all conditions of equilibrium (force and moment) provide the most accurate answers. These include Spencer's Method (Spencer 1967) and the Morgenstern and Price Method (Morgenstern and Price 1963). Most of the commercially available computer programs can perform these two methods.

In some cases, the potential critical failure surface may be easily identified by a feature such as a thin weak seam. In most other cases, it is necessary to search for the critical failure surface. The common slope stability programs have very robust search routines for circular and noncircular failure surfaces.

Figure 7-4 shows the formulas and calculations for a slope stability analysis using Bishop's Simplified Method. In this method, the soil mass is divided into vertical slices. The free body diagram for a slice is shown on the figure. This method uses circular failure surfaces, and the side forces are assumed to be horizontal. Moment equilibrium is satisfied, but only equations for vertical force equilibrium are used. Horizontal force equilibrium is not satisfied.
key_points: Limit equilibrium analysis divides the sliding mass into free bodies and applies force/moment equilibrium to compute F using Eq. 7-1.
Failure surfaces can be linear, circular, or combined linear and arc segments; in many cases iteration must be performed, and it takes a computer program to apply the method efficiently.
Spencer's Method and Morgenstern-Price Method satisfy all equilibrium conditions and provide the most accurate answers.
Bishop's Simplified Method uses circular failure surfaces, vertical slices, horizontal side forces, and satisfies moment and vertical force equilibrium only.
In some cases the critical failure surface may be easily identified by a feature such as a thin weak seam; in most other cases it is necessary to search for it.
Most commercial slope stability programs include Spencer's and Morgenstern-Price methods and robust failure surface search routines.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing quantitative slope stability analysis using the limit equilibrium approach, including selection of method, failure surface type, and use of computer programs.

sections.title: Finite Element Analysis of Slopes
sections.summary: Describes the finite element (FE) and finite difference methods for slope stability, which use a strength reduction factor (SRF) instead of the traditional factor of safety. The SRF reduces cohesion and tan(φ) until the solution no longer converges. Key advantages include automatic identification of the critical failure surface and full satisfaction of equilibrium equations.
sections.body:
Use of finite element analysis to analyze slope stability is becoming more popular in geotechnical practice. A thorough assessment of the use of the finite element method is presented by Griffiths and Lane (1999). The finite difference method is an alternative to the finite element method, and both of these assess the slope in a similar fashion. Instead of calculating a factor of safety as defined by Equation 7-1, the finite element and finite difference solutions use a strength reduction factor (SRF). The SRF is a factor by which the cohesion (c) and the tangent of the friction angle (φ) are reduced to a point where the solution no longer converges. At the critical SRF, the displacements increase rapidly and the equations for equilibrium can no longer be solved.

The finite element method has a few advantages over the more common limit equilibrium method. The failure surface does not have to be identified prior to the analysis. The FE method actively seeks out the critical failure surface automatically as part of the analysis procedure. In addition, the equations for equilibrium are satisfied.
key_points: FE and finite difference methods use a strength reduction factor (SRF) rather than the traditional F = s/τ definition.
SRF reduces cohesion c and tan(φ) until the numerical solution no longer converges, identifying the critical state.
At critical SRF, displacements increase rapidly and equilibrium equations cannot be solved.
FE method automatically identifies the critical failure surface without pre-specification.
In the finite element method the equations for equilibrium are satisfied.
Griffiths and Lane (1999) provide a thorough assessment of FE application to slope stability.
sections.applicability: Applies when considering finite element or finite difference methods as alternatives to limit equilibrium for slope stability analysis.

sections.title: Limit Analysis
sections.summary: Introduces limit analysis for slope stability based on upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity theory. The method analyzes the failure mass using kinematically admissible velocity fields and statically admissible stress fields. Though available for over 40 years, it has seen limited use in practice; commercially available programs are now emerging and may increase its popularity.
sections.body: Limit analysis is based on the upper and lower bound theorems for the theory of plasticity. The process involves section of a potential failure surface, and analyzing the failure mass based on a kinematically admissible velocity field and a statically admissible stress field. The use of limit analysis for slope stability calculations has been around for over 40 years, but it has found limited use in geotechnical engineering practice. Commercially available programs that use limit analysis have recently become available, and the popularity may increase.
key_points: Limit analysis is based on upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity theory.
Analyzes failure mass using a kinematically admissible velocity field and a statically admissible stress field.
Has been available for over 40 years but has seen limited adoption in geotechnical engineering practice.
Commercially available programs implementing limit analysis are now emerging, potentially increasing its use.
sections.applicability: Applies when considering limit analysis, based on the upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity, as an alternative slope stability method.

sections.title: WATER PRESSURE EFFECTS
sections.summary: Covers the two categories of water pressures affecting slope stability — internal (pore water) pressures and external pressures — explaining when each applies in effective stress vs. total stress analyses. Internal pressures act on the failure plane and are used only with effective stress parameters; external pressures apply to the free body surface and are included in both analysis types.
sections.body:
Water pressures have a profound effect on the stability of slopes. As an example, many failures that occur in natural and constructed slopes occur during periods of heavy precipitation. There are two categories of water pressures in slope stability analysis: (1) internal water pressures and (2) external water pressures. Examples of these are shown in Figure 7-5.

Internal water pressures are the same as pore water pressures. These are the static or dynamic water pressures that act on the failure plane within the soil mass. Internal water pressures must be included in slope stability analyses where the soil is characterized by effective stress or drained shear strength parameters (c′ and φ′). Internal water pressures are not included in the analysis where the soil is characterized by total stress or undrained shear strength parameters (su or c and φ).

External water pressures are the pressures applied to the free body where standing water is in contact with the soil mass at locations other than the failure surface. Examples of external water pressures are the pressures applied by the reservoir on the upstream slope of a dam or water-filled tension cracks. External water pressures are included in both effective stress and total stress slope stability analyses.
key_points: Two categories of water pressures affect slope stability: internal (pore water) pressures and external pressures.
Internal water pressures act on the failure plane and are only included when using effective stress (drained) shear strength parameters (c′ and φ′).
Internal water pressures are NOT used in total stress / undrained analyses (su or c and φ).
External water pressures act on the free body surface (e.g., reservoir on a dam upstream slope, water-filled tension cracks) and are included in BOTH effective stress and total stress analyses.
Water pressures have a profound effect on slope stability; many failures in natural and constructed slopes occur during periods of heavy precipitation.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever performing slope stability analysis where water pressures — either pore water or standing external water — are present.

sections.title: Incorporating Water Pressures in Computer Analyses
sections.summary: Describes how water pressures are specified in slope stability software, which the engineer should fully understand and verify: water table, phreatic surface and piezometric surface, and five ways to enter internal water pressures (water table or phreatic surface, piezometric surface, finite element seepage analysis, point-by-point x-y entry, pore pressure coefficient ru). Finite element seepage analysis is probably the best; ru is perhaps the least accurate. External water pressures can be applied through the water table, distributed loads, or a soil material with the unit weight of water and no strength.
sections.body:
It is important that the engineer fully understand the way that water pressures are specified in computer programs that they use, and how to verify that the correct water pressures are being used. The nomenclature for inputting water pressures is not consistent between the many different programs available for slope stability analysis.

The water table or groundwater table is normally defined as a line that connects points where the pore water pressure (u) is equal to zero. Water table is often used synonymously with phreatic surface. The piezometric surface is a surface connecting the height or elevation that water would rise in a series of standpipe piezometers. For hydrostatic conditions with a horizontal water table, the water table, phreatic surface, and piezometric surface are the same. For hydrodynamic cases where water is flowing, the piezometric surface can be at a higher elevation than the water table (upward flow of water) or at a lower elevation than the water table (downward flow of water). An example of this is shown in Figure 7-6. At Point A, the vertical distance to the phreatic surface is indicated on the drawing. However, the pore water pressure is controlled by the distance to the piezometric line, which is also shown on the figure.

Internal water pressures can be accommodated in slope stability software in one or more of the following methods:
(1) Water table or phreatic surface – can be corrected to approximate the piezometric surface based on the slope of the surface above the specific point,
(2) Piezometric surface,
(3) Finite element seepage analysis,
(4) Point-by-point entry in x-y coordinates with subsequent interpolation between points, and
(5) Pore pressure coefficient, ru.

Of these different methods, the finite element seepage analysis is probably the best. It allows a large density of pore water pressure points to be calculated and interpolation between these points is sufficiently accurate with most interpolation methods. Use of the pore pressure coefficient is perhaps the least accurate of the methods listed and is normally only used to verify results from historic analyses.

External water pressures can be automatically applied by most programs by the use of the water table or phreatic surface. As an alternative, external water pressures can be applied by the use of triangular and rectangular distributed loads. A third method is to assign the water properties of a soil material, having the unit weight of water but no shear strength. External water pressures in tension cracks are normally handled automatically by the computer program, but triangular distributed loads can also be used to model water-filled tension cracks.
key_points: Nomenclature for water pressure input varies among slope stability programs; it is important that the engineer fully understand how the programs specify water pressures and how to verify that the correct water pressures are being used.
The water table (phreatic surface) is where pore water pressure u = 0; under hydrostatic conditions it coincides with the piezometric surface.
Under hydrodynamic (seepage) conditions, the piezometric surface diverges from the phreatic surface: higher for upward flow, lower for downward flow.

Five methods exist for specifying internal pore pressures in software: (1) water table/phreatic surface, (2) piezometric surface, (3) finite element seepage, (4) point-by-point x-y entry, and (5) pore pressure coefficient ru.

Of these methods, finite element seepage analysis is probably the best: it gives a large density of pore water pressure points, and interpolation between them is sufficiently accurate with most methods.
Use of the pore pressure coefficient ru is perhaps the least accurate of the methods and is normally only used to verify results from historic analyses.

External water pressures can be applied by most programs through the water table or phreatic surface, by triangular and rectangular distributed loads, or by a soil material with the unit weight of water and no shear strength; water in tension cracks is normally handled automatically.
sections.applicability: Applies when using computer software for slope stability analysis where internal pore water pressures must be defined and verified.

sections.title: Seepage Forces
sections.summary: Defines the seepage force imparted to soil by flowing water, S = i · γw (Eq. 7-2), a force per volume where the head loss occurs. Flow parallel to a slope face can reduce the factor of safety to about half of that without flowing water. Seepage forces with buoyant unit weights require hand calculation; current programs instead use total unit weights below the water table with boundary water pressures, the method used in practice.
sections.body:
The flow of water through a slope can serve to destabilize slopes. As indicated in Figure 7-1, the flow of water parallel to the surface of a slope can reduce the factor of safety to about half of the factor of safety without flowing water. As water flows through a soil, a seepage force (S) is imparted to the soil from the viscous resistance to the flow of water. The seepage force can be calculated from:

S = i · γw   (7-2)

where:
i = hydraulic gradient, and
γw = unit weight of water.

The seepage force equation provides a force per volume for the volume where the hydraulic gradient or head loss occurs. For slope stability analyses, the effect of flowing water can be handled by (1) calculating the seepage forces for each slice or free-body and (2) using the buoyant unit weight of the soil below the phreatic surface. Unfortunately, using this method requires that the calculations be largely done by hand. The computer programs that are commercially available do not perform these calculations automatically. The alternative method, which is accommodated by current computer programs, correctly calculates the factor of safety of slopes where flow is occurring by using total unit weights of soils below the water table along with boundary water pressures as discussed above. This method is currently used in geotechnical engineering practice.
key_points: Flow of water parallel to the surface of a slope can reduce the factor of safety to about half of the factor of safety without flowing water (Figure 7-1).
Seepage force S = i · γw (Eq. 7-2), a force per volume for the volume where the hydraulic gradient or head loss occurs.

Using seepage forces for each slice with buoyant unit weights below the phreatic surface requires that the calculations be largely done by hand; commercial programs do not perform these calculations automatically.
Current programs correctly calculate the factor of safety with flow by using total unit weights below the water table along with boundary water pressures; this method is currently used in practice.

equations.description: Seepage force imparted to soil by flowing water: S = i · γw, where i is the hydraulic gradient and γw the unit weight of water; a force per volume for the volume where the hydraulic gradient or head loss occurs.

sections.applicability: Applies when the destabilizing effect of water flowing through a slope is considered in a slope stability analysis.

sections.title: STRENGTH MODELS AND ANALYSIS CASES
sections.summary: Introduces slope stability analysis cases, often categorized as undrained (total stress, short-term) or drained (effective stress, long-term) according to the time required for the soil to consolidate under the changed loading; both kinds of strength parameters can be assigned to different soils in one cross section depending on their drainage condition. The general analysis cases follow (7-6.1 to 7-6.5).
sections.body: Slope stability analysis cases are often categorized as undrained (or total stress) or drained (effective stress) analyses. These are often called short-term and long-term analyses because their respective use is related to the amount of time required for the soil to consolidate under the changed loading. For this reason, both effective stress and undrained (total stress) strength parameters can be assigned to the different soils in a cross section depending on their drainage condition during the duration of loading. The general analysis cases are listed below with guidance on strength models to be employed with each.
key_points: Analysis cases are broadly categorized as undrained (total stress, short-term) or drained (effective stress, long-term).
Strength parameter selection depends on the drainage condition of each soil during the loading duration.
Both effective stress and undrained parameters may coexist in the same cross section for different soil layers.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever selecting strength models and analysis cases for slope stability analyses.

sections.title: End of Construction (Short Term)
sections.summary: Covers end of construction (short-term) analysis, after construction and before dissipation of pore water pressures in fine-grained soils. Example: a compacted clay embankment over saturated fine-grained soils (Figure 7-7a); the partially saturated embankment is a c-φ soil with parameters from UU triaxial tests, and the saturated in situ soils are φ = 0, su = c, measured by UU triaxial, DSS, laboratory miniature vane, field vane, and under some conditions CPT tests.
sections.body: End of construction or post-construction analyses are performed to examine the stability after construction is completed and prior to any dissipation of pore water pressures in fine-grained soils. An example of a valid end of construction analysis is construction of a compacted clay embankment over saturated fine-grained soils. A cross section of this is shown in Figure 7-7a. For this case, the compacted clay embankment would be partially saturated, and the strength would be represented as a c-φ soil, with the strength parameters determined from UU triaxial tests. The in situ fine-grained soils would be essentially saturated, and the strength would be characterized as φ = 0, su = c. The shear strength of the in situ soils could be measured by UU triaxial tests, DSS tests, laboratory miniature vane shear tests, field vane shear tests, and under some conditions, cone penetration tests.
key_points: Applies after construction is complete but before pore pressure dissipation in fine-grained soils.
Compacted clay embankment treated as partially saturated c-φ soil; strength parameters from UU triaxial tests.
In situ saturated fine-grained soils modeled with φ=0 (undrained), su=c.
In situ strength could be measured by UU triaxial, DSS, laboratory miniature vane shear, field vane shear, and under some conditions cone penetration tests.
sections.applicability: Applies to stability analysis of embankments over fine-grained soils immediately after construction, before pore pressure dissipation.

sections.title: Cut Slope in Clay
sections.summary: Addresses cut slopes in stiff clay (Figure 7-7b), where the critical time is long after the cut, when the phreatic surface has reached steady state; effective stress (drained) strengths should be used. Low plasticity clays (LL < 40 and PI < 20): peak c′ and φ′ from CU triaxial or CD direct shear tests. High plasticity, fissured and/or heavily overconsolidated clays: fully softened shear strength, measurable on remolded specimens in direct shear. Non-linear envelopes are appropriate.
sections.body: The cross section of a cut slope in a stiff clay is shown in Figure 7-7b. The critical time in the performance of the cut slope occurs long after the cut is made, when the phreatic surface has reached a steady-state condition. For this type of scenario, effective stress or drained shear strengths should be used for the clay. If the clay has a relatively low plasticity (LL < 40 and PI < 20), it would be appropriate to use the peak drained strength parameters (cʹ and φʹ) determined from CU triaxial tests or CD direct shear tests. The use of a non-linear effective stress envelope for the clay would also be appropriate (Duncan et al. 2014). If the clay has a high plasticity, contains fissures, and/or is heavily overconsolidated, then the fully softened shear strength should be used to account for changes in shear strength that will likely occur over time. The fully softened shear strength can be measured using remolded test specimens in a direct shear apparatus. Again, the use of a non-linear envelope would be appropriate.
key_points: Critical stability condition for cut slopes in clay is long-term, after the phreatic surface reaches steady state.
Effective stress or drained shear strengths should be used for the clay in this analysis.
Low-plasticity clays (LL < 40, PI < 20): use peak c′ and φ′ from CU triaxial or CD direct shear tests.
High-plasticity, fissured, or heavily overconsolidated clays: use fully softened shear strength from remolded direct shear tests.
Non-linear effective stress envelopes are appropriate for both cases.
sections.applicability: Applies to long-term stability analysis of cut slopes in stiff clay once the phreatic surface has reached steady state.

sections.title: Steady State Seepage in Dams
sections.summary: Covers stability analysis of earth and rockfill dam slopes under steady-state seepage conditions, assuming the reservoir has been at a constant elevation long enough for a steady seepage pattern to develop. Pore pressures are computed via finite element analysis; effective stress parameters c′ and φ′ are used throughout the dam and foundation. Strength parameters are determined from CD direct shear, CD triaxial, or CU triaxial tests on compacted specimens.
sections.body: One of the stability analyses required for earth and rockfill dams is the evaluation of the factor of safety for the condition of steady state seepage (Figure 7-7c). This case assumes that the reservoir has been at a relatively constant elevation for long enough that a steady-state seepage pattern has developed. The pore water pressures in the dam and foundation can be calculated using finite element analysis. The pore pressures above the phreatic surface are normally assumed to be equal to zero. Effective stress strength parameters (cʹ and φʹ) are used in the dam and foundation soils. The effect stress strength parameters for the dam materials can be measured with CD direct shear, CD triaxial, or CU triaxial tests on compacted test specimens. In the example, the strength parameters for the silty sand can be determined using in situ tests.
key_points: Steady-state seepage condition assumes constant reservoir elevation long enough for a stable seepage pattern.
Pore water pressures can be calculated using finite element analysis; pressures above the phreatic surface are normally assumed equal to zero.
Effective stress parameters c′ and φ′ used for dam and foundation soils.
Dam material strength measured by CD direct shear, CD triaxial, or CU triaxial tests on compacted specimens.
In situ tests used to determine strength parameters for foundation soils such as silty sand.
sections.applicability: Applies to stability analysis of earth and rockfill dam slopes under steady-state seepage conditions.

sections.title: Stabilizing Berm for Failed Slope
sections.summary: Describes stability analysis of slopes stabilized with a berm at the toe after failure in fat clay. When sufficient displacement has occurred on the known failure surface, residual shear strength (φ′r or nonlinear residual envelope) is the appropriate parameter, measured by ring shear tests on remolded specimens. This is an effective stress analysis with the appropriate phreatic surface.
sections.body: Berms are often used to stabilize failed slopes. For example, Figure 7-8 is a cross section of a slope that failed in a fat clay. A stability berm has been constructed at the toe of the slope to increase the factor of safety. It is presumed that the failure surface is known based on inclinometer readings or borings. If sufficient displacement has occurred on the failure surface, then the appropriate shear strength to use is the residual shear strength. The residual friction angle (φʹr) or a nonlinear residual effective stress envelope is best determined by ring shear tests conducted on remolded test specimens of the fat clay. This should be an effective stress analysis with the appropriate phreatic surface used in the analysis.
key_points: Stability berms are used to increase the factor of safety of failed slopes.
If sufficient displacement has occurred on the failure surface, the appropriate shear strength to use is the residual shear strength.
Residual friction angle φ′r or nonlinear residual envelope is best determined from ring shear tests on remolded specimens.
Analysis should be an effective stress analysis with an appropriate phreatic surface.
The failure surface is presumed known from inclinometer readings or borings.
sections.applicability: Applies to effective stress stability analysis of a failed slope stabilized with a berm, where sufficient displacement on the known failure surface makes residual shear strength appropriate.

sections.title: Other Analysis Cases
sections.summary: Summarizes additional complex slope stability cases including rapid drawdown for earth/rockfill dam upstream slopes and seismic/earthquake loading. Rapid drawdown uses a three-stage analysis with a complex strength model; effective stress rapid drawdown methods based on uncoupled transient seepage should be avoided. Earthquake analyses range from simple pseudostatic to complex numerical methods. Both require experienced engineers.
sections.body:
Many other analysis cases are analyzed in geotechnical engineering practice that can be significantly more complex than the simple examples provided. For earth and rockfill dams, a critical case for the upstream slope is rapid drawdown. This occurs when the steady state seepage condition is changed by lowering the reservoir. If the reservoir is lowered rapidly (meaning days or weeks), the upstream slope no longer has the stabilizing support of the external water pressure. The shear strengths in the dam are based on the effective stresses prior to drawdown, and the lowering of the reservoir can cause an undrained failure. This is normally performed as a three-stage analysis, and it uses a strength model that is more complex than those used in the other cases described above (Duncan et al. 2014). These types of require considerable technical ability and they should be performed by engineers who have experience with rapid drawdown analysis. Effective stress rapid drawdown methods, such as those based on uncoupled transient seepage analyses, should be avoided.

The stability of slopes is also analyzed for cases of earthquake loading. These analyses can range from simple pseudostatic methods, where a horizontal force is applied to the free body of the limit equilibrium analysis, to very complex numerical analyses. Earthquake analyses are another category that require considerable judgment and experience to obtain meaningful results and should be conducted by engineers skilled in this branch of geotechnical engineering.
key_points: Rapid drawdown is a critical upstream slope case for earth/rockfill dams; reservoir lowering over days/weeks removes stabilizing water pressure and can cause undrained failure.
Rapid drawdown is typically a three-stage analysis requiring a complex strength model; should be performed by experienced engineers.
Effective stress rapid drawdown methods based on uncoupled transient seepage analyses should be avoided.
Earthquake stability analyses range from simple pseudostatic (horizontal force applied to free body) to complex numerical methods.
Both rapid drawdown and seismic analyses require significant engineering judgment and experience.
sections.applicability: Applies to complex slope stability cases including rapid drawdown of earth/rockfill dams and earthquake loading analyses.

sections.title: Back-Analysis of Slopes
sections.summary: Explains how back-analysis of failed slopes (where F=1 is known) allows determination of shear strength parameters or pore pressure conditions at failure. For undrained failures, average undrained shear strength is obtained; for drained failures, only one effective stress parameter (typically φ′ assuming c′=0) can be determined. It is important that the other parameters (slope geometry, soil stratigraphy, unit weights, etc.) be known with confidence, and for drained failures the pore pressures at the time of failure; the location of the failure surface should also be known, often from inclinometer readings or by careful drilling and sampling.
sections.body:
Failed slopes offer a unique opportunity to develop a model of the shear strengths and ground water conditions at the time of failure. This type of model can be very useful in designing slope stabilization or in analyzing nearby slopes. When performing a forward analysis, the most important unknown is the factor of safety for a specific failure surface. When conducting a back-analysis of a slope, the factor of safety is known (F = 1), so a different unknown can be calculated. Normally, the shear strength of a soil layer is the desired property to be determined from back-analysis. If the back-analysis is performed on a slope that failed in an undrained condition, then the average undrained shear strength of a soil layer can be determined from the analysis. If the back-analysis is performed on a slope that failed in a drained condition, then only one of the effective stress strength parameters (cʹ or φʹ) can be determined. Often, the effective stress cohesion is assumed to be equal to zero, and the friction angle is calculated.

It is important that the other parameters used in a forward analysis be known with confidence for back-analysis. These include the slope geometry, soil stratigraphy, shear strength parameters for layers where strengths are not back-calculated, unit weights, etc. For back-analysis of drained failures, it is important that the pore pressure conditions at the time of failure be known. The location of the failure surface should also be known to obtain the most accurate results. Often, the failure surface location may be known from the results of inclinometer readings. In other cases, the location of the failure plane can be determined by careful drilling and sampling. If only the head scarp and toe exit of the failure plane is known, then the failure surface can be determined from the computer program's search routine by only searching for surfaces which go through those two points. If the position of the failure surface is not known, it is important to search for the critical surface and not to assume the location. If the location of the failure surface is assumed, then the resulting shear strength back-calculated will be too low.
key_points: In back-analysis the factor of safety is known (F = 1), so a different unknown can be calculated, normally the shear strength of a soil layer.
Undrained failure back-analysis yields average undrained shear strength of the failing soil layer.
Drained failure back-analysis can determine only one effective stress parameter; c′ is typically assumed zero and φ′ is solved.

It is important that the other parameters (slope geometry, stratigraphy, strengths of layers not back-calculated, unit weights) be known with confidence; for drained failures, the pore pressure conditions at the time of failure.
Failure surface location should be known (from inclinometers or drilling); assuming the location results in back-calculated shear strength that is too low.
If only head scarp and toe exit are known, the computer search should be constrained to surfaces passing through those two points.
sections.applicability: Applies when using a documented slope failure to back-calculate shear strength parameters or groundwater conditions for use in stabilization design or analysis of adjacent slopes.

sections.title: Evaluation of Slope Stability Results
sections.summary: Gives guidance on evaluating computer slope stability results. Hand verification is impractical for complex methods, so Wright (2013) suggested that specifications require a second program to analyze the same failure surface with the same method; correct analyses agree within about 1%. Slice forces between slices and at slice bases should be in compression, and the line of thrust should lie within the soil mass. Non-convergence can cause critical surfaces to be missed, and the engineer should check for it before analyses for record.
sections.body:
Limit equilibrium slope stability calculations involve thousands of calculations. Since the adoption of computer programs to perform these calculations, project specifications often required that hand calculations be used to verify the results of the computer analyses. While this was possible when simpler methods of slope stability were used, such as Bishop's Simplified Method and the Ordinary Method of Slices, this requirement became impractical for more complex methods, like Spencer's Method and Morgenstern and Price's Method. The time required to perform the calculations by hand for one failure surface for a cross section containing many slices and an advanced shear strength model has become excessive. In recognition of this, Wright (2013) suggested that new project specifications should require that two different slope stability computer programs should be used to verify analyses. After the minimum factor of safety for the critical failure surface is determined using one program, a different program should be used to analyze the same failure surface using the same method. If the analyses are correct, the factors of safety calculated should be within about 1% of each other.

It is important for the engineer to be able to examine the forces acting on each slice. In particular, the forces at the boundary between slices should be in compression, and the normal force at the base of the slice should be in compression. Many computer programs allow the line of thrust to be plotted on the cross section. The line of thrust is a line that is plotted at the point of application of each of the side forces. Ideally, the line of thrust should be located within the soil mass defined by the slices. If portions of the line of thrust plot outside of the free body being analyzed, it often indicates tensile forces between slices or tensile forces at the base of slices. The addition of tension cracks to the cross section can be used to prevent tensile forces between slices, and these can be readily accommodated in commercial computer programs. Further information regarding the utility of the line of thrust can be found in Whitman and Bailey (1967).

The search routines for common commercial slope stability computer programs analyze thousands to tens of thousands of failure surfaces. The stability methods that solve for all conditions of equilibrium have iterative solutions, and the solutions do not always converge. There can be various reasons why the solutions do not converge, including geometry issues with invalid failure surfaces, problems with interpolation of advanced strength models, numerical issues with the solution procedure, etc. Critical failure surfaces can be missed as a result of non-convergence. The engineer should be able to identify when convergence issues are present. The location of this information varies depending on the program that is used, and is sometimes difficult to find. Prior to performing any analyses for record, the engineer should find this information and assess the validity of their results.
key_points: Hand verification is impractical for complex methods (Spencer, Morgenstern and Price); Wright (2013) suggested that specifications require two different slope stability programs to verify analyses.
Two programs analyzing the same failure surface with the same method should produce factors of safety within ~1% of each other.
Inter-slice and base normal forces should be compressive; tensile forces indicate potential model problems.
The line of thrust should fall within the soil mass; portions outside the free body indicate tensile inter-slice or base forces.
Tension cracks can be added to prevent tensile inter-slice forces in commercial programs.

Iterative solutions do not always converge, and critical failure surfaces can be missed; before analyses for record, the engineer should find the convergence information and assess the validity of the results.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating, verifying, and quality-checking results from computer-based limit equilibrium slope stability analyses.

sections.title: Slope Stability Charts
sections.summary: Describes the history, uses, and limitations of slope stability chart solutions. Charts cover drained, undrained, rapid drawdown, infinite slope, surcharge, and tension crack cases. An example infinite slope analysis chart is shown (Figure 7-9). While modern computer programs have reduced the speed advantage of charts, they remain a viable complementary method for simple soil profiles and straightforward strength interpretations; accuracy decreases for complex profiles.
sections.body:
Chart solutions for slope stability analyses have been available since the 1930s. Prior to the introduction of computers into geotechnical engineering practice, slope stability charts allowed an approximate solution to be quickly obtained. The charts are also useful in estimating the critical failure circle, showing the mode of failure (toe circle vs. deep circle), and other valuable information.

Charts have been developed for many different categories of slope stability analysis, including drained analyses, undrained analyses, rapid drawdown analyses, infinite slope analyses, surcharge loading at the crest, tension cracks, and other specialty cases. A comprehensive set of chart solutions can be found in Duncan et al. (2014). An example of a chart for infinite slope analysis is shown in Figure 7-9. Infinite slope analysis is useful for explaining sloughing failures for slopes having an effective stress cohesion equal to zero, and to examine the effects of seepage on the factor of safety of slopes.

Charts have historically been used to obtain a quick solution to slope stability problems. Even with the advent of computer-based slope stability analyses, chart solutions still provided an approximate factor of safety in less time than required to run a computer analysis. However, the modern computer programs allow slope stability problems to be defined and solved very quickly, and the speed advantage of chart solutions has been diminished. Chart solutions are best suited for slope stability problems that have simple soil profiles and straightforward strength interpretations. As the soil profiles and strength interpretations become more complex, the accuracy of chart solutions decreases. Even so, chart solutions still offer a viable complementary analysis method to computer solutions.
key_points: Slope stability charts have been available since the 1930s and cover many analysis types: drained, undrained, rapid drawdown, infinite slope, surcharge, and tension cracks.
Charts are useful for estimating critical failure circles and identifying failure mode (toe vs. deep circle).
Infinite slope charts (Figure 7-9) are particularly useful for sloughing failures with c′=0 and for examining seepage effects.
Modern computer programs solve slope stability problems very quickly, and the speed advantage of chart solutions has been diminished.
Charts remain best suited for simple soil profiles and straightforward strength interpretations; accuracy decreases with complexity.
Chart solutions serve as a viable complementary check against computer-based analyses.
sections.applicability: Applies when using chart solutions as a quick or complementary slope stability analysis method, best suited to simple soil profiles and straightforward strength interpretations.

sections.title: SLOPE STABILIZATION
sections.summary: Covers methods for increasing the factor of safety of existing slopes and repairing slopes that are moving or have failed. References Figure 7-10, which illustrates the various slope stabilization techniques available to engineers when addressing unstable or failing slope conditions.
sections.body: It is often necessary to increase the factor of safety of existing slopes or to repair slopes that are moving or have failed. Figure 7-10 shows different methods of stabilizing slopes.
key_points: It is often necessary to increase the factor of safety of existing slopes or to repair slopes that are moving or have failed.
Multiple stabilization methods exist; Figure 7-10 provides a visual overview of the available techniques.
sections.applicability: Applies when an engineer must evaluate, repair, or improve the stability of an existing slope that is failing or at risk of failure.

sections.title: Required Factor of Safety for Soil Slopes
sections.summary: Covers required minimum factors of safety for soil slopes, often set by municipal or government organizations: for earth dams, values recommended by USACE EM 1110-2-1902 (Table 7-2) and by USBR (Table 7-3, Spencer's method). The required minimum depends on the type of structure and analysis, consequences of failure, uncertainty in design parameters and frequency of loading; it may depend on whether conditions are well-defined or poorly-defined, a classification requiring engineering judgment. An uncited example guideline requires 1.25 with sufficient characterization and 1.5 otherwise.
sections.body:
There are many different sources that specify the minimum factor of safety. Often, the design values are determined by municipal or government organizations. For earth dams, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' EM 1110-2-1902 (2003) recommends the values listed in Table 7-2. Other organizations dealing with earth dams, such as the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR), have specified their own values. The values recommended by USBR are given in Table 7-3.

The required minimum factor of safety is dependent on many different factors, including: (1) type of structure, (2) type of analysis, (3) consequences of failure, (4) uncertainty involved with design parameters, (5) frequency of specific loading event, and many others. An important concept in arriving at a minimum factor of safety involves the degree of uncertainty associated with the design parameters. Sometimes, the minimum factor of safety depends on if the analysis has “well-defined conditions” or “poorly-defined conditions.” Engineering judgment is required to classify a particular site or project into one of these two categories. In some cases, the designation of “well-defined conditions” can only be applied for sites that have already been built upon. In general, well-defined conditions means that the site exploration and field or laboratory testing program was thorough enough for the engineer to have confidence in the soil stratigraphy and shear strength interpretation. A poorly-defined condition can occur when the borings are spread far apart, few laboratory tests have been conducted, and/or the soil stratigraphy is highly variable.

An example of this is the geotechnical guidelines for a large Washington DC suburb. The requirements for factors of safety for two different soil formations are given as follows [Footnote 13: This example is intentionally left uncited to maintain anonymity of the source.]: “For long-term stability, a minimum Factor of Safety (FS) of 1.25 is required when supported with sufficient field and laboratory characterization of the slope’s soils. Otherwise, a minimum FS of 1.5 is required. In case of Critical slope or structure, a minimum FS of 1.5 is required unless a laboratory measured residual strength test is obtained and used in the analysis. In this case, a minimum FS of 1.25 is required when supported with sufficient field and laboratory characterization of the soils.” “For long-term stability of the soil formations other than Potomac Formation clay if slope stability analysis is deemed necessary by the engineer or if it is required by the County, a minimum Factor of Safety (FS) of 1.25 is only acceptable when the slope is not critical and the analysis is supported with sufficient site-specific in situ or laboratory strength tests of the encountered soils. Otherwise, a minimum factor of safety of 1.5 must be used in the analysis.”
key_points: Many different sources specify the minimum factor of safety; often the design values are determined by municipal or government organizations.

USACE EM 1110-2-1902 (2003) recommends Fmin = 1.3 (end of construction), 1.5 (steady state seepage, downstream), 1.4 (maximum pool, downstream) and 1.1 to 1.3 (rapid drawdown, upstream) for new earth and rockfill dams (Table 7-2).
USBR 2011 specifies Fmin using Spencer's Method ranging from 1.2 to 1.5 depending on loading condition, shear strength parameters, and pore pressure characteristics.
The highest USBR value is Fmin = 1.5, for steady-state seepage under active conservation pool with effective shear strength parameters.
Rapid drawdown conditions (USBR) carry Fmin of 1.2–1.3 depending on whether drawdown is from normal or maximum water surface.
The required minimum factor of safety depends on the type of structure, type of analysis, consequences of failure, uncertainty in design parameters, frequency of the loading event, and other factors.

Well-defined conditions: exploration and testing thorough enough for confidence in stratigraphy and strength; poorly-defined: borings far apart, few laboratory tests and/or highly variable stratigraphy; classifying a site requires engineering judgment.

Example guideline (uncited): long-term FS of 1.25 with sufficient field and laboratory characterization, otherwise 1.5; for a critical slope or structure, 1.5 unless a measured residual strength is used.

sections.title: Mechanically Stabilized Earth Slopes
sections.summary: Introduces MSE technology as applied to earth slopes, distinguishing it from MSE retaining walls. Covers the scope of the section — providing rudiments of design and analysis for evaluating outside designs — and references DM 7.2 for MSE retaining wall design. Notes that design/analysis of MSE slopes is a specialty area in geotechnical engineering.
sections.body:
Mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) is a term that refers to soil retention structures that include both retaining walls and earth slopes. This section discusses the application of MSE technology to slopes. The design of MSE retaining walls is discussed in DM 7.2.

Design and analysis of MSE slopes is a specialty area in geotechnical engineering. There are engineering consultants who specialize in MSE walls and slopes. In this manual, the rudiments of design and analysis are presented in order that outside designs can be evaluated and not for the purpose of completing a full MSE design.
key_points: MSE encompasses both retaining walls and earth slopes; this section discusses the application of MSE technology to slopes.
MSE retaining wall design is covered separately in DM 7.2.
The manual presents rudiments for evaluating outside MSE designs, not for performing complete MSE design.
MSE slope design is a specialty area; engineering consultants often specialize in this work.
sections.applicability: Applies when an engineer needs to understand the scope and purpose of MSE slope coverage in this UFC.

sections.title: Applications of MSE
sections.summary: Describes the structure of MSE slopes including reinforced, retained, and foundation soil zones. Explains the roles of primary and secondary reinforcement, identifies primary limitations (constructability and utilities), and defines the FHWA face-angle threshold (θ = 70°) distinguishing MSE slopes from MSE walls, with implications for land use efficiency.
sections.body:
Reinforced earth slopes are fill structures in which discrete layers of geosynthetic or steel elements are installed during construction at specified locations. A typical cross section of an MSE slope is shown in Figure 7-11.

The reinforced soil zone is that portion of the slope in which layers of reinforcement are installed. The retained soil zone and foundation soil zone are located behind and below the reinforced soil zone, respectively. The layers of primary reinforcement shown in Figure 7-11 resist the development of failure planes through the reinforced soil zone. The layers of secondary reinforcement prevent surficial failure at the slope face.

The primary limitations on the use of MSE slopes relate to constructability and utilities. Constructability is not typically an issue if the slope is part of a larger fill area but may be a concern when an existing hillside must be excavated to build the slope. Utilities can be significant factors in the poor performance of MSE structures, particularly if the utility is wet such as a storm sewer or water main. The malfunction of wet utilities may contribute to about one-third of the failures of MSE retaining walls (Valentine 2013).

The distinction between an MSE retaining wall and an MSE slope has been defined by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) based on the face angle, θ (FHWA 2009b). If θ < 70°, then the structure is a slope. If θ ≥ 70° or greater, then the structure is a wall. The distinction between an MSE retaining wall and slope has important implications for land use efficiency as illustrated in Figure 7-12. However, the increased land use efficiency of MSE walls and slopes is accompanied by complications related to facing requirements and structural deformations, as well as increased cost.
key_points: MSE slopes consist of reinforced, retained, and foundation soil zones; primary reinforcement resists internal failure planes; secondary reinforcement prevents surficial face failure.
FHWA defines MSE slope vs. wall by face angle θ: θ < 70° is a slope; θ ≥ 70° is a wall.
The malfunction of wet utilities (storm sewers, water mains) may contribute to about one-third of the failures of MSE retaining walls (Valentine 2013).
Constructability is generally acceptable for fill areas but may be an issue when excavating existing hillsides.
Greater land use efficiency of steeper MSE structures comes with higher costs and facing/deformation complications.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting MSE slopes for fill or hillside construction and when distinguishing MSE slope from MSE wall configurations.

sections.title: Reinforced Slope Materials
sections.summary: Specifies fill soil and geosynthetic material requirements for MSE slopes. Provides grading and plasticity index criteria for reinforced fill based on slope geometry (Table 7-4), and summarizes all components — reinforcement, facing, internal drainage, and external drainage — with materials and purposes (Table 7-5). Applicable to slopes with H < 70 ft.
sections.body:
The soil that is installed in the reinforced zone of an MSE slope is an important structural component of the slope. The properties that are required of reinforced soil should be based on the geometry of the slope and the structures that may depend on the slope for support. FHWA's recommendations for the properties of fill soil in the reinforced zone of MSE slopes permit up to 50% fines that have a PI ≤ 20 (FHWA 2009b). The fill properties shown in Table 7-4 are recommended for relatively tall or steep slopes; however, the recommendations are only applicable to slopes with a height less than 70 feet.

Other important components of MSE walls and slopes include internal and external drains, filters, separators and erosion control. The use of geosynthetics for these applications is summarized in Table 7-5.
key_points: Reinforced fill properties should be based on the geometry of the slope and the structures that may depend on it for support; FHWA permits up to 50% fines with PI ≤ 20.
For slopes < 1.2H:1V (θ < 40°) and H < 70 ft: No. 200 sieve allows up to 50% passing, PI ≤ 20.
For slopes 1.2H:1V to 0.36H:1V (40° ≤ θ ≤ 70°) and H < 70 ft: No. 200 sieve limit is 0–35% passing, PI ≤ 10.
Table 7-4 fill recommendations apply only to slopes H < 70 ft.
PET and HDPE are usually used for primary reinforcement; PET, HDPE and PP can be used for secondary reinforcement (Table 7-5).
Internal drainage uses gravel (ASTM C33 No. 57 or No. 67) with nonwoven PP geotextile; external drainage uses TRM-lined swales located 5–10 ft behind slope crest.
Hard armor facing (θ ≥ 40°) typically uses galvanized WWF 4x4-W4.0xW4.0 with hardware cloth and gravel fill behind it.
