sections.title: Geosynthetic Reinforcement Strength
sections.summary: Covers how the design tensile strength of geosynthetic reinforcement is established for MSE slopes. Explains MARV basis, uniaxial vs. biaxial behavior, and the application of three reduction factors (creep, durability, installation damage) to obtain the long-term allowable strength Tal per FHWA procedures.
sections.body:
Geosynthetics that are used in soil reinforcement applications are typically designed to exhibit their maximum tensile strength in one direction. In this respect, such geosynthetics are said to be uniaxial and the design strength direction usually corresponds to the material's MD or roll-direction. Geosynthetics that exhibit significant tensile strength in both the MD and cross machine direction (XMD) are said to be biaxial.

The tensile strength of a geosynthetic that is used for the design of an MSE slope is based on a minimum average roll value (MARV) that is reported by the manufacturer. In the United States, the industry practice is to reduce the average value by two standard deviations and to define the result as the minimum average roll value (MARV). Reduction factors are then applied to the strength MARV to account for potential degradation of strength as a result of creep, environmental conditions and installation damage.
key_points: Geosynthetic design tensile strength is based on MARV, defined as the average minus two standard deviations.
Uniaxial geosynthetics provide maximum strength in one direction (MD/roll direction); biaxial provide strength in both MD and XMD.
Three reduction factors applied to MARV: RFCR (creep), RFD (durability/environment), RFID (installation damage).
Details on determining each reduction factor are in FHWA (2009b) Appendix B.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the design tensile strength of geosynthetic reinforcement for MSE slopes using FHWA procedures.

sections.title: Long-Term Design Strength
sections.summary: Defines the FHWA procedure for calculating the long-term allowable tensile strength (Tal) of geosynthetic reinforcement using Eq. 7-3. Tal is obtained by dividing the ultimate MARV strength by three reduction factors accounting for creep (RFCR), environmental degradation (RFD), and installation damage (RFID).
sections.body:
The assessment of a geosynthetic's long-term tensile strength (Tal) for use in the design of an MSE slope follows current FHWA procedures (FHWA 2009b):

Tal = TULT / (RFCR × RFD × RFID)  (7-3)

where:
TULT = ultimate tensile strength of the geosynthetic based on the MARV,
RFCR = reduction factor applied to account for creep under sustained tensile loading,
RFD = reduction factor applied to account for the degradation due to environment, and
RFID = reduction factor applied to account for damage during installation.

The reduction factors are discussed briefly in the following sections. Details regarding the determination of RFCR, RFD, and RFID for a geosynthetic can be found at Appendix B of FHWA (2009b).
key_points: Eq. 7-3 gives Tal = TULT / (RFCR × RFD × RFID).
TULT is based on MARV (average minus two standard deviations) as reported by the manufacturer.
The three reduction factors are multiplied together in the denominator of Eq. 7-3.
Detailed reduction factor determination procedures are in FHWA (2009b) Appendix B.

equations.description: Long-term allowable tensile strength of geosynthetic: Tal = TULT / (RFCR × RFD × RFID), where TULT is ultimate MARV strength, RFCR is the creep reduction factor, RFD is the durability reduction factor, and RFID is the installation damage reduction factor.

sections.applicability: Applies when computing the allowable long-term geosynthetic tensile strength for use in MSE slope design per FHWA procedures.

sections.title: Reduction Factor for Creep (RFCR)
sections.summary: Explains creep, the elongation of geosynthetics (PET, HDPE, PP and other polymers) under sustained tensile load, which can induce rupture or compromise performance. The US standard of practice bases RFCR on the sustained load that will induce creep rupture at the end of the design service period, which should be no less than 75 years for permanent MSE slopes; a longer period may be appropriate for structures supporting critical infrastructure.
sections.body:
The tendency of a geosynthetic to elongate under sustained tensile loading is called creep and it is a property of materials that are manufactured using PET, HDPE, PP and other polymers. If the magnitude of the load is sufficiently great and if it is maintained for a sufficient period of time, the creep can induce rupture or result in such elongation that the material's performance is compromised.

In the United States, the standard of practice is to determine a reduction factor for creep (RFCR) that is based on the sustained load that will induce creep rupture at the end of the design service period. For permanent MSE slopes the design service period should be no less than 75 years. A longer service period may be appropriate for structures that support critical infrastructure.
key_points: Creep is time-dependent elongation of polymeric geosynthetics under sustained load; can lead to rupture or performance loss.
RFCR is based on the sustained load inducing creep rupture at the end of the design service period.
The design service period for permanent MSE slopes should be no less than 75 years; a longer period may be appropriate for structures that support critical infrastructure.
All common reinforcement polymers (PET, HDPE, PP) are subject to creep.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the creep reduction factor RFCR for geosynthetic reinforcement in permanent MSE slopes with a design life of at least 75 years.

sections.title: Reduction Factor for Durability (RFD)
sections.summary: Describes environmental degradation mechanisms for geosynthetic reinforcement: hydrolysis for PET, oxidation (including UV-oxidation) for HDPE and PP. Notes FHWA default RFD of 1.3 for PET, HDPE, and PP where certain criteria are met, with the option for lower values from product-specific testing. Protective measures to limit UV exposure are also addressed.
sections.body:
Geosynthetics may degrade depending on their base polymer and if they are exposed to certain environmental conditions. Polyester geosynthetics may degrade as a result of hydrolysis. Geosynthetics manufactured with HDPE and PP are subject to degradation by their reaction with oxygen, particularly in the presence of elevated temperatures. Oxidation can also be initiated by exposure to UV light (i.e., UV-oxidation). The resistance of these polymers to oxidation can be significantly increased by the addition of antioxidants during the manufacturing process. Polyester is also susceptible to UV-oxidation but to a lesser degree than HDPE and PP (FHWA 2009a). Protection of PET yarns is typically provided in the form of coatings. In the case of all geosynthetics, the protective roll wraps should not be removed until the material is installed to minimize UV light exposure.

The FHWA recommends a default reduction factor for durability (RFD) of 1.3 for PET, HDPE, and PP geosynthetics provided certain criteria are satisfied. Also, a lower RFD may be used if it is indicated by product specific testing. Further details are given in FHWA (2009b).
key_points: Polyester (PET) may degrade by hydrolysis; HDPE and PP are subject to oxidation, particularly at elevated temperatures, and UV-oxidation; PET is also susceptible to UV-oxidation to a lesser degree.
Antioxidant additives during manufacturing significantly increase resistance to oxidation for HDPE and PP.
FHWA default RFD = 1.3 for PET, HDPE, and PP when specified criteria are met; lower values permitted with product-specific testing.
Protective roll wraps should remain on geosynthetics until installation to minimize UV exposure.
Protection of PET yarns is typically provided in the form of coatings.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or verifying the durability reduction factor RFD for geosynthetic reinforcement exposed to environmental degradation in MSE slopes.

sections.title: Reduction Factor for Installation Damage (RFID)
sections.summary: Describes how RFID is assessed through manufacturer full-scale testing involving compaction of various soil types. Provides construction practice guidelines to minimize installation damage: minimum 8-inch soil cover for tracked equipment, rubber-tire speed limits, and proper fill placement procedures (dozer-bladed, not dumped directly on geosynthetic).
sections.body:
The standard of practice in the United States is for the manufacturers of geosynthetic reinforcement to assess the potential for installation damage through the performance of full-scale tests. Such testing programs typically evaluate the damage induced by compaction of coarse gravel, sandy gravel and silty or clayey sand.

The geosynthetic manufacturer should be consulted to obtain its recommendation for the reduction factor for installation damage (RFID). The manufacturer should also be consulted for its recommendations regarding measures to reduce installation damage. Typical measures include the following:
• Tracked vehicles should not traffic directly on panels of geosynthetic reinforcement. There should be no less than 8 inches of fill soil between the tracks and the geosynthetic. Sharp turns by tracked vehicles on fill soil should be avoided.
• Rubber tire vehicles may operate directly on the geosynthetic reinforcement at speeds less than 10 miles per hour. Sudden braking and turning should be avoided.
• Fill soil should not be dumped directly onto geosynthetic reinforcement. Rather, it should be dumped onto fill soil that has already been spread and then bladed onto the geosynthetic by a dozer.
key_points: RFID is determined by the geosynthetic manufacturer through full-scale installation damage testing with coarse gravel, sandy gravel, and silty/clayey sand.
There should be no less than 8 inches of fill soil between tracked vehicles and the geosynthetic; tracked vehicles should not traffic directly on it, and sharp turns should be avoided.
Rubber tire vehicles may operate directly on the geosynthetic at speeds less than 10 miles per hour; sudden braking and turning should be avoided.
Fill soil should not be dumped directly onto the geosynthetic; it should be dumped onto spread fill and bladed onto the geosynthetic by a dozer.
Consult manufacturer for both RFID value and specific installation damage mitigation measures.
sections.applicability: Applies during construction of MSE slopes when specifying construction practices and obtaining the installation damage reduction factor RFID for geosynthetic reinforcement.

sections.title: Soil-Geosynthetic Interaction
sections.summary: Defines geosynthetic pullout resistance Pr = F*·α·σʹv·Le·C (Eq. 7-4, FHWA 2009b), the coefficient of interaction Ci = tan δ / tan φʹ (Eq. 7-5) used by some manufacturers, and F* = Ci·tan φʹ (Eq. 7-6). Reinforcement length is based in part on pullout resistance; Le is calculated for the surface with the minimum acceptable F and should be no less than 3 feet.
sections.body:
The determination of geosynthetic reinforcement length in the design of an MSE slope is based in part on the resistance of the reinforcement to pullout from between layers of confining soil. In FHWA (2009b) the FHWA defines a geosynthetic's resistance to pullout as:

Pr = F* · α · σʹv · Le · C  (7-4)

where:
Pr = geosynthetic reinforcement's resistance to pullout,
F* = pullout resistance factor,
α = scale correction factor to account for nonlinear stress reduction,
σʹv = effective vertical stress at the soil-reinforcement interface,
Le = length of reinforcement embedded behind the trial failure surface, and
C = number of surfaces on which pullout resistance is mobilized (i.e. 2 for geosynthetics).

The critical failure surface used to calculate Le should be that surface that exhibits the minimum F deemed acceptable. Also, Le should be no less than 3 feet to assure adequate pullout resistance.

Some manufacturers of geosynthetic reinforcement have characterized soil-geosynthetic interaction in terms of a coefficient of interaction (Ci) based on pullout tests with Ci defined as:

Ci = tan δ / tan φʹ  (7-5)

where:
φʹ = the effective stress internal angle of friction, and
δ = the effective soil-geosynthetic interface friction angle.

The values of F* and Ci are related by:

F* = Ci · tan(φʹ)  (7-6)
key_points: Pullout resistance Pr (Eq. 7-4) depends on pullout resistance factor F*, scale correction α, effective vertical stress σʹv, embedded length Le, and number of pullout surfaces C (=2 for geosynthetics).
Le should be no less than 3 feet to assure adequate pullout resistance.
Le is calculated for the critical failure surface exhibiting the minimum acceptable F.
Coefficient of interaction Ci = tan δ / tan φʹ (Eq. 7-5); relates interface friction to soil friction.
F* and Ci are related by F* = Ci · tan(φʹ) (Eq. 7-6), allowing conversion between the two characterizations.

equations.description: Geosynthetic pullout resistance: Pr = F* × α × σʹv × Le × C, where F* is the pullout resistance factor, α is the scale correction factor, σʹv is the effective vertical stress, Le is the embedded reinforcement length behind the failure surface, and C is the number of pullout surfaces (2 for geosynthetics).
Coefficient of interaction: Ci = tan δ / tan φʹ, where δ is the effective soil-geosynthetic interface friction angle and φʹ is the effective stress internal friction angle of the soil.
Relationship between pullout resistance factor and coefficient of interaction: F* = Ci × tan(φʹ).

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating geosynthetic reinforcement pullout resistance and determining required embedment length Le in MSE slope design.

sections.title: Analysis and Design of Reinforced Slopes
sections.summary: Addresses limit equilibrium analysis of MSE slopes, including selection of analysis methods (Spencer's or Morgenstern-Price preferred), failure surface types (circular, noncircular, compound, global), and two methods (A and B) for incorporating geosynthetic strength in the factor of safety equation. Provides a 15-step computer modeling procedure (Table 7-7) and references Table 7-6 for FS equation formulations.
sections.body:
The most technically challenging aspect of the design of an MSE slope is deciding the required strength, length and vertical spacing of the layers of reinforcement. The critical failure surface for a slope with layers of horizontally-oriented geosynthetic reinforcement is frequently a combination of circular and linear segments, particularly if the critical failure surface is entirely outside of the reinforced soil zone (i.e., a global failure surface rather than a compound failure surface).

Most of the software packages that are used for soil slopes can also be used for MSE slopes. There are some software packages specifically written for MSE slopes, and these are listed in Appendix B. Spencer's Method (Spencer 1967) and the Morgenstern and Price Method (Morgenstern and Price 1963) both lend themselves to the analyses of noncircular failure surfaces, solve for all conditions of equilibrium (i.e. moment and force), and provide the most accurate solutions. Either of these two methods is preferred for the analysis of MSE slopes.

One of the most important considerations in the modeling of an MSE slope in a limit equilibrium slope stability computer program is the definition of F given in Equation 7-1. However, the presence of geosynthetic reinforcement requires that its strength be applied to the right side of the equation in the numerator or the denominator (Duncan et al. 2014). Two options are available as summarized in Table 7-6. The method used by slope stability software can be determined using the simple approach suggested by Duncan et al. (2014).

If Method A is used to define F, then the strength of the geosynthetic used to calculate F is Td. To account for potential uncertainties in the geosynthetic Td should be divided by a factor of safety for geosynthetic strength (FR) of at least 1.3. If Method B is used, then Td will be reduced by F and the application of FR is not necessary.

The reinforcement force orientation assumed by limit equilibrium analysis can vary from one that is parallel to the reinforcement to one that is tangent to the slip surface. Setting the orientation parallel to the reinforcement in a slope stability computer program is common practice and tends to result in a lower F compared to setting the orientation tangent to the slip surface.

A detailed discussion of the procedure to determine the reinforcement requirements of MSE slopes is provided by the FHWA (2009), particularly for the case in which Bishop's simplified method is used. The FHWA manual also considers the mechanics of internal sliding failure and locally soft foundation soil at the slope toe. The steps provided in Table 7-7 are intended to help an engineer to construct a computer model for an MSE slope design.

Using the process in Table 7-7, the modifications required to obtain a satisfactory F that is balanced with geosynthetic efficiency is an iterative process in which geosynthetic strengths and lengths are adjusted. Once the optimum design is determined, the parameters that may have significant uncertainty should be considered. For example, if rock is thought to be present below the toe of the MSE slope, changing the elevation of the top of rock by a few feet in the computer model can have a profound effect that makes the difference between a stable slope and slope failure. Similarly, there is frequently significant uncertainty regarding the location of groundwater and soil shear strength. The effect of these uncertainties should be investigated through parametric analyses coupled with engineering judgment. The designer is cautioned to avoid making the design over-complicated. Small savings in material obtained from optimized lengths or spacings are often offset by potential for error in construction or an increased difficulty in constructability.
key_points: Spencer's Method and Morgenstern-Price Method are preferred for MSE slope analysis due to noncircular capability and full equilibrium (moment + force) solutions.

The critical failure surface with horizontal geosynthetic layers is frequently a combination of circular and linear segments, particularly for a global failure surface entirely outside the reinforced soil zone.

Method A subtracts reinforcement resistance from the denominator, Method B adds it to the numerator. With Method A, Td should be divided by a factor of safety for geosynthetic strength (FR) of at least 1.3; with Method B, Td is reduced by F and FR is not necessary.
Reinforcement force orientation set parallel to reinforcement (common practice) yields lower F than tangent to slip surface orientation.

Table 7-7: a vertical reinforcement spacing of 3 ft is a good initial starting point and in general should not be exceeded; set each layer length L to about 0.7·H, more with a toe slope or crest slope.

Table 7-7 gives 15 steps for the computer model: analyze surfaces exiting through the slope face first, then compound and global surfaces below the toe; for a low compound F strengthen or tighten the lower layers, for a low global F lengthen the layers.
If Ci is unknown and unsupported by test data, assume Ci = 0.67 (conservative for fill shown in Table 7-4).

Reaching a satisfactory F balanced with geosynthetic efficiency is iterative; uncertain parameters (top of rock, groundwater, shear strength) should be investigated by parametric analyses with engineering judgment, and over-complicated designs avoided.
tables: Table 7-6: Methods of Incorporating Geosynthetic Reinforcement Strength in Factor of Safety Equation (p. 373) - columns: Method of Including Reinforcement Strength; Factor of Safety Equation. Method A (Active); F = shear strength / (shear stress required for equilibrum − reinforcement resistance) [as printed; 'equilibrum' for equilibrium] | Method B (Passive); F = (soil strength+reinforcement resistance) / (shear stress required for equilibrium)

Table 7-7: Steps for Designing an MSE Slope (p. 374) - columns: Step; Procedure. 1; Draw a scaled cross section of the slope that reflects the existing and proposed grades as well as external water conditions, and permanent and temporary loads. Use high quality site plans to locate these features as accurately as possible. | 2; Use the available geotechnical information to determine and draw the boundaries of soil and rock strata as well as groundwater. | 3; Use the results of Steps 1 and 2 it to construct the cross section in a computer program model. | 4; Assign physical, strength and hydraulic properties to the sections of the model as indicated by the available geotechnical information. | 5; Select either Spencer’s method or the Morgenstern and Price method to analyses failure surfaces. | 6; Select one to three values of geosynthetic reinforcement strength (Tal) based on manufacturer information, or assume typical values. | 7; Determine whether the computer program used Method A or B to defined F. If the program provides an option, select Method A and then reduce the geogrid strength by FR = 1.3 or more. | 8; Set the reinforcement force orientation parallel to the reinforcement. | 9; Assign the F* or Ci parameter based on recommendations by the manufacturer of the geosynthetic reinforcement. If recommendations are not available or if they are not supported by test data, assume that Ci = 0.67. This will be conservative for the soil parameters shown in Table 7-4. | 10; If the computer program provides an option, select 100% reinforcement coverage as opposed to partial coverage. | 11; Assign layers of geosynthetic reinforcement to the cross section. Vertical spacing of 3 ft. is a good initial starting point. In general, the vertical spacing of reinforcement should not exceed 3 ft. | 12; Set the length (L) of each layer of reinforcement to about 0.7·H. The required L will increase if there is a slope below (i.e., a toe slope) or behind (i.e., a crest slope) the MSE structure. | 13; Perform preliminary analysis by setting the search limits to evaluate only those surfaces which exit through the face of the slope. Evaluate both circular and noncircular failure surfaces. If the resulting F is too low, then change the layers in the vicinity of the bottom of the failure surface to types with higher strengths. | 14; After designing for failure surfaces that exit through the slope face, change the search limits to evaluate compound and global surfaces that pass below the toe of the structure. | 15; If a compound failure surface is indicated that has an unacceptably low F, then increase the strength of the lower reinforcement layers or decrease their vertical spacing. If a global failure surface is indicated that has an unacceptably low F, then increase the length of the reinforcement layers.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing limit equilibrium analysis and computer modeling for the design of geosynthetic-reinforced MSE slopes.

sections.title: Required Factor of Safety for MSE Slopes
sections.summary: Defines the target factor of safety for MSE slopes, based on uncertainties in site conditions and material properties and the consequences of failure: generally 1.3 to 1.5. A minimum F of 1.3 may be appropriate for well-understood conditions with relatively low consequences; F of 1.5 or higher may be necessary for poorly understood or changeable conditions, or indicated where important structures depend on the slope. MSE slopes designed in accordance with FHWA guidance require a minimum of 1.5.
sections.body: An MSE slope should be designed to a target F that is based on considerations of the uncertainties regarding site conditions, material properties and the consequences of slope failure. In general, the standard of practice is to provide a F in the range of 1.3 to 1.5. If the site conditions and material properties are understood well and if the consequences of failure are relatively low, then a minimum F of 1.3 may be appropriate. However, if site conditions are subject to unforeseeable changes and if soil types, strengths and locations are poorly understood, then F of 1.5 or higher may be necessary. Similarly, if the proper performance of the MSE slope is required for the operation of important structures, then F of 1.5 or higher may be indicated. For MSE slopes designed in accordance with FHWA guidance, a minimum factor of safety of 1.5 is required.
key_points: Target F for MSE slopes ranges from 1.3 to 1.5 based on site uncertainty and failure consequences.
A minimum F of 1.3 may be appropriate if site conditions and material properties are understood well and the consequences of failure are relatively low.

F of 1.5 or higher may be necessary if site conditions are subject to unforeseeable changes and soils are poorly understood, and may be indicated where proper performance is required for important structures.
FHWA-guided MSE slope designs require a minimum F of 1.5.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the required factor of safety for MSE slope design, especially under FHWA guidance.

sections.title: Rock Slope Stability
sections.summary: Introductory overview of rock slope stability for excavations related to roads, buildings, and infrastructure. Covers when stability issues arise during or after excavation, introduces the fundamental failure modes (sliding blocks, plane failure, wedge failure, toppling), and references stabilization measures and rock fall mitigation covered in subsequent subsections.
sections.body:
The stability of rock slopes may become a concern during the excavation for the construction of roads, buildings and infrastructure components. Often a stability issue cannot be identified until the excavation is underway and information that is needed to assess the potential for various modes of failure becomes available. Analyses of rock slope stability may need to be performed expeditiously to avoid project delays. The potential for delays can be exacerbated by a need to design stabilization measures. In other cases, rock slope instability does not occur until well after the initial excavation and rock weathering has taken its toll.

This section provides an overview of some of the aspects of rock slopes and a more in-depth discussion of others. The fundamental mechanics of rock slope failure are covered by a discussion of sliding blocks, plane failure, wedge failure, and toppling failure. Stabilization measures for rock slopes and mitigation of rock falls are also addressed. More in-depth discussion can be found in FHWA (1998), Hoek and Bray (1981), and Rowland et al. (2007).
key_points: Rock slope stability concerns often emerge during excavation for roads, buildings, and infrastructure.
Stability analyses may need to be performed quickly to avoid project delays.
Rock slope instability can also develop long after excavation due to weathering.
Key failure modes covered: sliding blocks, plane failure, wedge failure, toppling failure.
Key references: FHWA (1998), Hoek and Bray (1981), Rowland et al. (2007).
sections.applicability: Applies as an introduction whenever rock slope stability must be evaluated for excavations or long-term slope performance.

sections.title: Modes of Rock Slope Failure
sections.summary: Describes six typical rock slope configurations and the failure modes associated with each, including discontinuity-driven plane/wedge/toppling failures and weak-rock circular failures. Covers how discontinuity orientation (daylighting vs. non-daylighting), freeze-thaw, weathering sequences (sandstone/shale), and joint spacing govern failure risk.
sections.body:
Fortunately, the stresses in most rock slopes are much less than the rock strength, and for this reason most rock slopes are relatively stable. The potential for rock slope failure becomes a concern under two general conditions. First, discontinuities in the rock mass propagate and the rock separates as blocks, wedges, columns, or other types of sections. Second, rock that has already separated in the form of cobbles and boulders can translate downslope under the influence of gravity as a rock fall. In both cases, the separated rock may pose a hazard to both property and lives.

There are six typical configuration of rock slopes, some of which may pose risks of instability. Four possible configurations of rock discontinuities are shown in Figure 7-13 while rock slopes with weak and weathered rock are depicted in Figure 7-14.

The term discontinuity refers to faults, joints, bedding planes, or any other surface upon which rock may move. The pattern of discontinuities shown in Figure 7-13a is typical for sedimentary rock, such as limestone, sandstone, and shale, that has been deposited in bedded layers and later uplifted by geologic processes. The orientation of the discontinuities in Figure 7-13a is roughly parallel to the rock slope face, but they do not daylight at the slope face. That is, the discontinuities do not extend to and intersect the exposed surface of rock at the slope face. In such a configuration the rock slope face is expected to remain stable. In contrast, Figure 7-13b shows a rock slope with discontinuities that daylight at the slope face. With such orientation of discontinuities, a potential for rock slope failures exists.

Figure 7-13c shows a rock slope with generally favorable bedding in that the discontinuities dip into the rock slope and there is little potential for rock to slide out of the slope face. However, blocks of rock at the slope face may become instable when discontinuities daylight at the slope face. The potential for the development of such conditions are increased if blasting was performed during slope excavation.

A rock slope configuration that illustrates the conditions for the toppling of rock columns is shown in Figure 7-13d. Toppling becomes a risk for rock with relatively thin bedding with steeply dipping discontinuities. The stability of rock columns can degrade relatively quickly if water seeps readily into the discontinuities from surface water runoff and increases the rate of weathering. In regions with frequent freeze-thaw cycles the rate of degradation may accelerate further because the frozen water can cause the rock columns to separate.

Sandstone and shale are often found with near-horizontal bedding. Excavation of such a bedding sequence generally results in a shale layers that weather faster than sandstone. In such conditions layers of sandstone may be undermined and form ledges that are prone to fracturing and failure. Such a condition is illustrated in Figure 7-14a.

Weak rock slopes with closely spaced impersistent joints may fail along a circular or noncircular surface much like a soil slope as shown in Figure 7-14b.

An assessment of the potential for one of the above modes of failure to develop often requires a geologic investigation, field mapping of discontinuities, stereographic projection of geologic data, and an evaluation of rock strength. Each of these tasks represent significant sections in comprehensive publications on the topic of rock slope engineering.
key_points: Rock slope failure occurs due to propagation of discontinuities forming blocks/wedges/columns, or rock fall of already-separated material.
Discontinuities that do not daylight at the slope face generally indicate a stable slope; daylighting discontinuities indicate failure potential.

Toppling becomes a risk for rock with relatively thin bedding and steeply dipping discontinuities; degradation can be faster with water seeping into the discontinuities and frequent freeze-thaw cycles.
In near-horizontal sandstone and shale, the shale layers weather faster after excavation, and the sandstone may be undermined and form ledges prone to fracturing and failure (Figure 7-14a).
Weak rock with closely spaced impersistent joints may fail along circular/noncircular surfaces similar to soil slopes.
Assessing the potential for these modes often requires a geologic investigation, field mapping of discontinuities, stereographic projection of geologic data and an evaluation of rock strength.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying which mode of rock slope failure is relevant to a specific site based on discontinuity patterns and rock type.

sections.title: Mechanics of a Sliding Block
sections.summary: Presents the fundamental force equilibrium for a sliding rock block, defining weight components normal (FN) and parallel (FS) to the sliding plane as functions of the dip angle ΨP. Establishes the factor of safety against sliding assuming no pore pressure, and notes that positive pore pressure reduces effective normal stress and the factor of safety.
sections.body:
The mechanics of a sliding block are central to two types of rock slope stability analyses. Considering the rock slope depicted in Figure 7-15, the weight of the block ABC is represented by force W, which acts through the block's centroid. The component of W that acts perpendicular to the sliding plane AC is FN. The component of W that acts parallel to the sliding plane AC is FS. The relationship of these three forces is defined by the angle, or dip, of the sliding plane (ΨP) with respect to the horizontal plane.

The factor of safety against sliding on plane AC is calculated as shown in Figure 7-15. This solution assumes no pore pressure is acting on the sliding plane. Positive pore pressure will reduce the effective normal stress, shear strength, and the factor of safety.
key_points: Block weight W is decomposed into normal (FN) and parallel (FS) components relative to the sliding plane, governed by dip angle ΨP.
The factor of safety against sliding on plane AC is calculated as shown in Figure 7-15.
No pore pressure is assumed in the basic formulation; pore pressure reduces effective normal stress and lowers the factor of safety.
This sliding block model is foundational for both plane failure and wedge failure analyses.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing a basic factor of safety calculation for a rock block sliding on a planar surface with no pore pressure.

sections.title: Plane Failure
sections.summary: Describes plane failure as a specific case of the sliding block model, noting it is relatively rare due to strict geometric requirements. Emphasizes its instructional value for understanding wedge failure mechanics and introduces the conditions and orientation terminology needed for plane failure analysis.
sections.body: The rock slope with a sliding block shown in Figure 7-15 is a simple version of a plane failure. It is not a type of failure that is often encountered because the conditions for its development rarely occur. However, the mechanics of a plane failure also apply to the more frequently encountered wedge failure. For this reason, it is instructive to further consider plane failures.
key_points: Plane failure is a simplified and relatively rare rock slope failure mode requiring specific geometric conditions.
The mechanics of a plane failure also apply to the more frequently encountered wedge failure, so it is instructive to consider plane failures further.
Two subsections cover orientation terminology and the four geometric conditions required for plane failure.
sections.applicability: Applies as a container section when studying plane failure mechanics and their relationship to wedge failure analysis.

sections.title: Sloped Surface Orientation Terms
sections.summary: Defines the three key geometric terms used to describe planar orientations in rock slope analysis: dip (Ψ), dip direction/dip azimuth (α), and strike. Establishes that strike is perpendicular to dip direction, providing the vocabulary needed for plane and wedge failure assessments.
sections.body:
A discussion of plane failure requires the definition of three terms that are used to describe the orientation of sloped planes such as a slope face or a potential failure surface. The dip (Ψ) of a sloped plane is the inclination of that surface as measured from a horizontal plane, as shown in Figure 7-16. The dip direction or dip azimuth (α) is the direction of the horizontal trace of the line of dip measured clockwise from north.

Often the term strike is used to describe the orientation of a sloped plane. It is the direction of a line that is formed by an intersection of the sloped plane with an imaginary horizontal plane. The orientation of the strike of a sloped surface is perpendicular to the dip direction of the sloped surface.
key_points: Dip (Ψ) is the inclination of a plane measured from horizontal.
Dip direction or dip azimuth (α) is measured clockwise from north along the horizontal trace of the dip line.
Strike is the direction of intersection of the sloped plane with a horizontal plane; it is perpendicular to the dip direction.
A discussion of plane failure requires these three terms for the orientation of sloped planes such as a slope face or a potential failure surface.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever describing or analyzing the geometric orientation of rock discontinuities, slope faces, or failure planes.

sections.title: General Conditions for Plane Failure
sections.summary: Lists the four conditions that must be satisfied for sliding on a single plane (Hoek and Bray 1981): the plane strikes within about 20° of the slope face; it daylights in the slope face (ΨP < ΨF); its dip is greater than the angle of friction at the failure plane (printed 'φʹ < ΨF'; the words give φʹ < ΨP); and release surfaces with negligible resistance define the lateral boundaries (Figure 7-17).
sections.body:
For sliding to occur on a single plane the four conditions must be satisfied (Hoek and Bray 1981):
1. The plane on which sliding occurs must strike nearly parallel (i.e., within about 20º) to the slope face.
2. The failure plane must daylight in the slope face (i.e., intersect the slope face). Therefore, the dip of the failure plane (ΨP) must be less than the dip of the slope face, ΨF. That is, ΨP < ΨF.
3. The dip of the failure plane must be greater than the angle of friction at the failure plane. That is, φʹ < ΨF. [As printed (p. 380); the words of this condition compare the dip of the failure plane with the friction angle, so the evident reading is φʹ < ΨP.]
4. Release surfaces that provide negligible resistance to sliding must be present in the rock mass to define the lateral boundaries of the slide.
The relative positions of the planes defined by ΨF, ΨP, and φʹ are shown in Figure 7-17a. The release surfaces associated with a sliding plane are shown in Figure 7-17b.
key_points: Failure plane strike must be within ~20° of the slope face strike.
Failure plane must daylight at slope face: ΨP < ΨF.
The dip of the failure plane must be greater than the angle of friction at the failure plane; the print writes this as φʹ < ΨF (the words give φʹ < ΨP).
Lateral release surfaces with negligible sliding resistance must exist to define slide boundaries.
All four conditions must be met simultaneously for plane failure to develop.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing whether geometric conditions at a rock slope site are sufficient for plane failure to occur.

sections.title: Plane Failure Analyses
sections.summary: Covers the factor of safety calculation for plane failure including the effects of a tension crack (above or below the slope crest) that may contain water. Defines uplift force U at the failure plane and water force V in the tension crack, as shown in Figure 7-18. Notes that computer programs improve analytical efficiency over hand calculations.
sections.body:
Rock slopes analyzed for plane failure can also consider the presence of a tension crack, which may contain water. The crack may be located either above or below the slope crest as shown in Figure 7-18. The uplift force applied by water at the failure plane is designated as U. The force applied by water in the tension crack is designated as V. The factor of safety for such conditions can be calculated using the equation presented in Figure 7-18.

Further details regarding the stability analyses of sliding planes are described in the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981). While such analyses can be practically performed using hand calculations, analytical efficiency can be significantly improved by use of computer programs.
key_points: Plane failure analysis can incorporate tension cracks located either above or below the slope crest.
Water in the tension crack introduces force V; water on the failure plane introduces uplift force U.
The factor of safety accounting for U and V can be calculated using the equation presented in Figure 7-18.
Computer programs significantly improve efficiency over hand calculations for these analyses.
sections.applicability: Applies when computing the factor of safety for plane failure in rock slopes that may have tension cracks and/or water pressure on the failure plane.

sections.title: Wedge Failure
sections.summary: Describes wedge failure analysis for rock slopes where two intersecting discontinuity planes (Plane A and Plane B) define a sliding wedge. Introduces the wedge factor K relating wedge factor of safety FW to equivalent plane failure conditions, and notes that cohesion and water pressure require more complex analysis available in FHWA (1998) and Hoek and Bray (1981).
sections.body:
The rock slope with a sliding wedge shown in Figure 7-19 is similar to a sliding plane, but the presence of Plane A and Plane B make it possible to model a geometry that is encountered in the field more frequently.

The convention adopted in the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981) is that the release surface designated as Plane A is the flatter of the two release surfaces. The steeper release surface is designated as Plane B. These two surfaces intersect along the line of intersection.

As with a plane failure, there are certain geometrical requirements for wedge failure to occur. Specifically, ΨFi > ΨFi > φʹ [as printed (p. 381); the definitions that follow name Ψi as the dip of the line of intersection, so the evident reading is ΨFi > Ψi > φʹ], where ΨFi is the inclination of the slope face as measured at right angles to the line of intersection, Ψi is the dip of the line of intersection and φʹ is the average friction angle of Plane A and Plane B. Note that ΨFi is not the same as ΨF unless the dip direction of the line of intersection is the same as the dip direction of the slope face (Hoek and Bray 1981).

The factor of safety of the wedge in Figure 7-19 may be determined by assuming that sliding is resisted only by friction at the surface of Plane A and Plane B. With this simplifying assumption, the resisting forces on these planes can be determined by calculation of the normal forces RA and RB on each plane, as illustrated in Figure 7-20a. The component forces of the weight of the wedge perpendicular and parallel to the line of intersection are shown in Figure 7-20b.

Hoek and Bray (1981) relate the factor of safety against wedge failure (FW) to that for a slope with a face that is inclined at ΨFi and a failure plane that is inclined at Ψi by a wedge factor K. This wedge factor can be graphically determined using a figure provided in both the FHWA (1998) and Hoek and Bray (1981).

The analysis of a wedge failure for which cohesion or water are present is more complicated than for a wedge failure in which only the friction angle at the failure planes is considered. Both the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981) discuss this analytical process in detail. Such an analysis can also be performed efficiently using computer programs.
key_points: Wedge failure involves two intersecting release planes (Plane A = flatter, Plane B = steeper) forming a sliding wedge.

Geometric requirement printed as ΨFi > ΨFi > φʹ (the definitions give ΨFi > Ψi > φʹ), where ΨFi is the slope face inclination at right angles to the line of intersection, Ψi the dip of that line and φʹ the average friction angle of Planes A and B.
ΨFi differs from ΨF unless the line of intersection dip direction matches the slope face dip direction.
Basic analysis assumes friction only on Plane A and Plane B; normal forces RA and RB are computed from wedge weight components.
Wedge factor K relates FW to equivalent plane failure factor of safety; K is determined graphically.
Analysis with cohesion or water present is more complicated (FHWA 1998; Hoek and Bray 1981) and can also be performed efficiently using computer programs.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating factor of safety against wedge failure for a rock slope with two intersecting discontinuity planes.

sections.title: Toppling Failure
sections.summary: Explains toppling failure mechanics for rock columns where the center of gravity lies on the slope-face side, creating eccentric loading and tensile stress on the back face. Notes that toppling analyses are significantly more complex than plane or block failure and that hand calculation methods (FHWA 1998) may have limited applicability to field conditions.
sections.body:
For a column of rock to be subject to toppling failure, the center of gravity of the column must be located on the side of the column at the slope face. In this way, the column is loaded eccentrically. Such loading creates tensile stress on the side of the column away from the slope face, as shown in Figure 7-21. If the tensile capacity of the column is exceeded, failure can ensue.

Analyses of rock toppling can be significantly more complicated than those for plane failure or block failure. A method for hand calculations is described in FHWA (1998) but such a procedure may have limited applicability to actual field conditions.
key_points: Toppling occurs when the center of gravity of a rock column is on the slope-face side, creating eccentric loading.
Eccentric loading generates tensile stress on the back face of the column; failure occurs when tensile capacity is exceeded.
Toppling analyses are substantially more complex than plane or block failure analyses.
Hand calculation methods from FHWA (1998) exist but have limited applicability to real field conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing the risk of toppling failure for rock columns with steeply dipping, thin-bedded discontinuities at a slope face.

sections.title: Circular Failure
sections.summary: Addresses circular or noncircular failure of weak rock slopes with closely spaced impersistent joints, analogous to soil slope failure. Cautions that weak intact rock can still have significant cohesion, that cohesive strength is difficult to measure accurately, and that zones of stronger rock behind weaker zones may shift the location of the critical failure surface.
sections.body: As described in section 7-10.1, if a rock slope consists of weak material with closely spaced, impersistent joints, then the slope may fail along a circular or noncircular surface much as a soil slope. Analyses of these types of failures can be performed using the methods previously discussed for the stability of soil slopes. However, it should be noted that even weak intact rock can exhibit significant cohesive strength. An accurate assessment of the actual cohesive strength may be difficult to make. It is also important to realize that zones of relatively strong rock may exist behind zones of relatively weak rock. The presence of the strong rock zones may significantly affect the location of the critical failure surface.
key_points: Weak rock with closely spaced impersistent joints can fail along circular or noncircular surfaces similar to soil slopes.
Soil slope stability methods are applicable for these analyses.
Even weak intact rock may have significant cohesive strength that is difficult to measure accurately.
Zones of stronger rock behind weaker rock can significantly influence the location of the critical failure surface.
sections.applicability: Applies when analyzing failure of weak or closely jointed rock slopes where failure mode resembles soil slope circular failure.

sections.title: Rock Slope Stabilization and Protection
sections.summary: Introduces the range of measures available to mitigate hazards from unstable rock slopes, varying from simple to complex in terms of required analytical expertise, construction skill, and expense. Serves as a container section for subsections covering reinforcement, shotcrete, buttresses, drains, rock removal, rock fall protection, and rock sheds/tunnels.
sections.body: Several measures can be taken to mitigate the hazards presented by unstable rock slopes. These measures vary from the relatively simple to those which require considerable analytical expertise, construction skill, and expense.
key_points: Mitigation measures vary from the relatively simple to those requiring considerable analytical expertise, construction skill and expense.
Categories include rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers.
sections.applicability: Applies as an overview container when selecting and designing rock slope stabilization or protection measures.

sections.title: Stabilization and Protection Options
sections.summary: Summarizes the three primary categories of rock slope stabilization measures — rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers — and references Figure 7-22 which enumerates specific options within each category per FHWA (1998).
sections.body: The range of stabilization measures that are typically available include rock reinforcement, rock removal and protective barriers. A range of options is available under each of these categories as shown in Figure 7-22.
key_points: Three primary categories of stabilization: rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers.
Figure 7-22 (after FHWA 1998) enumerates specific options within each category.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and comparing available stabilization and protection options for an unstable rock slope.

sections.title: Reinforcement
sections.summary: Covers passive anchors (rock bolts/dowels, soil nails) and active anchors (stressed bar or strand tendons) for rock slope stabilization. Describes installation methods, typical bar sizes (No. 8–No. 11), tensile capacities (35–500+ kips for strand), grout vs. resin bonding, corrosion protection, and references FHWA GEC No. 7 and GEC No. 4. Includes electrochemical limits for corrosive environments.
sections.body:
Anchors have been used for many years to stabilize both soil and rock slopes. In general, anchors can be classified as passive or active. A passive anchor that is frequently used for top-down excavation stabilization is the soil nail. For rock slope stabilization it may be referred to as a rock bolt or dowel. It typically comprises a steel tendon in the form of an all-thread bar that is centered within a drill hole. A cement grout is installed in the drill hole to bond the tendon to the adjacent soil or rock. Grout is usually placed by tremie from the distal end to the anchor head. Typically, such holes are drilled at a declination of about 15° or more below the horizontal plane to prevent spilling of the grout at the excavated face.

The steel bars used for these applications typically exhibit a tensile capacity of at least 75 ksi. Higher capacity bars are readily available. Typical bar diameters correspond to standard reinforcement steel sizes of #8 (i.e. 1.0-inch nominal diameter) to #11 (i.e. 1.41-inch nominal diameter). Resistance to bar corrosion is typically provided by an epoxy coating or galvanization. The grout that surrounds the bar can also provide some protection against corrosion, but the grout is subject to cracking and may not provide complete coverage.

Different types of liquid resins are manufactured for use with rock anchors as an alternative to cement grout. Resin cartridges include a hardener that can be selected to provide a range of hardening times. The cartridges are inserted into the drill hole and then followed by insertion of the steel bar tendon. The tendon is then spun at a prescribed rate to mix the resin and hardening agent and to distribute the mixture to both bar and rock surfaces. Unfortunately, there is some skepticism within the ground anchor contracting industry that resins can be consistently distributed to rock and tendon surfaces and can reliably provide requisite bond capacities. Also, resins do not provide the same level of corrosion protection as does cement grout.

The FHWA has published several manuals on the design of soil nail structures. The current version is Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 7 (FHWA 2015). This manual should be consulted in the design of passive anchors for rock stabilization applications.

A passive anchor does not impart a stabilization force to the adjacent rock or soil until the rock or soil tends to displace. At that point the passive anchor provides a resisting force. In contrast, an active anchor is stressed as part of its installation process. Such anchors may comprise steel bars like a soil nail. However, if a particularly long anchor or one with high tensile capacity is required, then steel strand tendons may be indicated. The installation of such an active anchor is similar to that of a passive anchor. First, a hole for the anchor is drilled and then the strand is inserted and centered within the hole. Next, the strand is grouted, but only for a certain length of the strand starting from the distal end. A length between the top of the grouted section and the anchor head is left unbonded. The reason for the unbonded section is that this portion of the tendon must be left to strain under a design stressing load to provide an active force at the anchor head. This force is transferred to a loading plate or block that is secured against the rock slope face. In this way the active force can be used to stabilize a large rock plane, wedge or unstable columns. This is perhaps the most important distinction between an active anchor and a passive anchor. Unlike a passive anchor, an active anchor does not depend on soil or rock movement to mobilize its strength.

The bonded length of the tendon is that portion which is grouted. The length of the bonded section is based on analyses that consider the load in the anchor and the bond strength between the grout and the adjacent soil or rock.

Steel strand tendons are typically available in configurations that provide a working tensile capacity of about 35 to 500 kips. Tendons with considerably higher capacities can be fabricated.

The design of active anchor systems is discussed in the FHWA's Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 4 (FHWA 1999). This manual should be consulted in the design of active anchors for rock stabilization applications.

When anchors are designed for the stabilization of rock slopes, some consideration should be given to the potential for conditions that may cause steel corrosion. Such conditions often prevail in areas where coal and acidic runoff are present or where sodic and pyritic soils are found. The FHWA provides the electrochemical parameters in Table 7-8 as limits for the use of steel reinforcement in MSE structures. These limits should be considered when designing the corrosion protection for active and passive anchors.
key_points: Passive anchors (rock bolts/dowels/soil nails) mobilize resistance only when rock or soil tends to displace; active anchors are pre-stressed at installation.
Typical passive anchor bars: #8–#11 steel (1.0–1.41 in. diameter), ≥75 ksi tensile capacity; drilled at ≥15° declination to prevent grout spillage.
Active anchors use bonded + unbonded strand tendons; working capacity typically 35–500 kips; unbonded section allows pre-stressing.

There is some skepticism in the ground anchor contracting industry that resins can be consistently distributed and reliably provide requisite bond capacities; resins also do not provide the same corrosion protection as cement grout.
FHWA GEC No. 7 (FHWA 2015) should be consulted in the design of passive anchors and GEC No. 4 (FHWA 1999) in the design of active anchors for rock stabilization.

Consideration should be given to conditions that may cause steel corrosion (often where coal and acidic runoff or sodic and pyritic soils are present); the Table 7-8 limits should be considered when designing corrosion protection.
The active force can stabilize a large rock plane, wedge or unstable columns; unlike a passive anchor, an active anchor does not depend on soil or rock movement to mobilize its strength.

sections.applicability: Applies when designing passive or active anchor reinforcement systems for rock slope stabilization, especially in potentially corrosive environments.

sections.title: Shotcrete
sections.summary: Describes shotcrete (concrete with little to no gravel-size particles, sprayed in layers and reinforced with WWF or bars) for rock slopes subject to raveling and dislodgement of gravel, cobbles and boulders. It should be secured with relatively short passive anchors (10 feet or less if not needed for planes and wedges; spacing no greater than about 6 feet on mostly unstable faces) or it may delaminate. Water behind shotcrete is a common cause of separation; drainage composites (4 ft wide, 50% coverage) with drainage grates and weep holes should be used, especially where water can freeze.
sections.body:
Shotcrete is essentially concrete that has little to no gravel-size particles (i.e. larger than the No. 4 sieve) that can be sprayed onto vertical and near-vertical surfaces. It is usually applied in layers to build up the total coating to a specified thickness. Both steel welded wire fabric (WWF) and bars may be used within the shotcrete to provide reinforcement.

Shotcrete can be used to stabilize rock slopes that are subject to raveling and dislodgement of gravel, cobble and boulders. It will tend to adhere to such unstable faces but it should be secured with relatively short passive anchors (i.e. soil nails, rock bolts or dowels). Otherwise, the shotcrete may delaminate from the rock slope in a short period of time. The length of the anchors can be 10 feet or less if they are not actually needed for stabilization of rock planes and wedges. If the rock slope surface is mostly unstable then the anchors should be spaced at intervals no greater than about 6 feet.

A common cause for separation of shotcrete from the face of a rock slope is the presence of water behind the shotcrete. Water frequently seeps from rock slopes, and it should be drained using a drainage composite. Drainage is especially important in climates where the water can freeze. Drainage composites can be successfully used behind shotcrete. The composites typically are available in a width of 4 feet. They should be installed with a coverage of 50%. A drainage grate should be installed at the base of each drainage composite strip and daylighted by a weep hole through the shotcrete.
key_points: Shotcrete is essentially concrete with little to no gravel-size particles (larger than the No. 4 sieve), sprayed in layers onto vertical and near-vertical surfaces.

Shotcrete should be secured with relatively short passive anchors (10 feet or less if not needed for planes and wedges), spaced no greater than about 6 feet on mostly unstable faces; otherwise it may delaminate.
A common cause of separation of shotcrete is water behind it; water seeping from rock slopes should be drained using a drainage composite.
Drainage composites (typically 4 ft wide) should be installed with 50% coverage, with a drainage grate at the base of each strip daylighted by a weep hole through the shotcrete.
Drainage is especially important in climates where the water can freeze.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shotcrete face protection for rock slopes subject to raveling, dislodgement, or surface instability.

sections.title: Buttress
sections.summary: Describes buttresses as gravity structures providing passive resistance to rock slope displacement. Options include piled soil or rock, reinforced concrete structures, or MSE structures. Engineering analyses are analogous to gravity retaining wall design.
sections.body: Buttresses have been used for more than 1,000 years to stabilize slopes, walls and buildings. In general, a buttress is a gravity structure that provides passive resistance to displacement. For rock slope stabilization a buttress may comprise piled soil or rock, or it may be an engineered reinforced concrete structure or an MSE structure. The engineering analyses of the mass requirements of a buttress are relatively straightforward and similar to those of a gravity retaining wall.
key_points: A buttress is a gravity structure that provides passive resistance to displacement.
Options include piled soil/rock, reinforced concrete, or MSE structures.
Mass requirement analyses are similar to gravity retaining wall design.
sections.applicability: Applies when a buttress (piled soil or rock, reinforced concrete or MSE structure) is considered to provide passive resistance to rock slope displacement.

sections.title: Drains
sections.summary: Covers relief drains for rock slopes, which are drilled at ≥2° above horizontal (opposite to anchors) to dissipate pore pressures. Notes the practical limitation that relief drains frequently become clogged by organic material and that removal of obstructions is generally not practical.
sections.body:
Drains are often used in conjunction with rock slope reinforcement measures to counter the destabilizing effects of water that is retained behind a slope face. In general, relief drains are drilled using equipment similar to that used for anchors. However, instead of being angle below the horizontal plane relief drains are typically angle 2° or more above the horizontal plane.

An unfortunate reality of relief drains is that they often become clogged by the accumulation of organic material. Removal of the organic obstructions is generally not practical.
key_points: Relief drains counter the destabilizing effects of water retained behind a slope face and are typically angled 2° or more above the horizontal plane.
Drilling equipment is similar to anchor installation equipment.
Relief drains often become clogged by the accumulation of organic material, and removal of the obstructions is generally not practical.
sections.applicability: Applies when installing relief drains to reduce water pressure behind a rock slope face, typically used in conjunction with reinforcement.

sections.title: Rock Removal
sections.summary: Describes three scales of rock removal for slope stabilization: mass excavation (drilling, blasting, heavy equipment), selective trimming of overhangs and problematic formations, and scaling to remove loose cobbles and boulders presenting rock fall hazards. Notes cost and disruption tradeoffs between mass excavation and trimming.
sections.body:
The stability of rock slopes can often be improved by the removal of material. On a large scale, such removal may take the form of mass excavation using drilling and blasting measures followed by dozers, track hoes and haul trucks.

On a smaller scale trimming may be used to more selectively remove problematic formations such as overhangs (see Figure 7-14), planes, wedges and columns. Trimming may also employ drilling and blasting and may be preferable to mass excavation in terms of cost and also in terms of potential disruption of adjacent transportation or commercial operations.

If the rock slope includes loose cobbles and boulders that may present a rock fall hazard, then scaling may be the most appropriate method of rock removal. In a scaling operation, personnel traverse the slope face while secured by ropes and harnesses. They use hand tools to dislodge rock and may even remove soil deposits and vegetation.
key_points: Mass excavation uses drilling, blasting, dozers, track hoes, and haul trucks for large-scale removal.
Trimming selectively targets overhangs, planes, wedges, and columns; may be preferred over mass excavation for cost and reduced disruption.
Scaling removes loose cobbles and boulders using rope-secured personnel with hand tools; appropriate for rock fall hazard mitigation.
sections.applicability: Applies when rock removal is the chosen stabilization strategy for overhangs, loose material, or overall slope geometry correction.

sections.title: Rock Fall Protection Measures
sections.summary: Covers rock fall protection: surface restraints, barriers and ditches, whose design usually requires an assessment of rock fall risk. Rock fall analyses are generally beyond hand calculations; when FHWA (1998) was published, computer modeling had to be paired with videography and surveying for meaningful accuracy. Capture ditches are dimensioned per FHWA (1998); steel face mesh is anchored on the face or draped from a stable section with a ditch below, with corrosion protection; catch fences are practical and cost-effective but need a trajectory assessment.
sections.body:
Measures to protect against rock falls may include the installation of surface restraints, barriers or ditches. However, the design of any of these measures usually requires an assessment of the risk posed by rock falls.

Rock fall analyses are generally beyond the capabilities of hand calculations, although some graphical aids have been developed for this purpose (FHWA 1998). When the FHWA (1998) was published, the computer-supported analysis of rock falls was at a relatively early stage. The complexity of the problem was such that computer modeling had to be paired with videography and surveying to render solutions with meaningful accuracy.

After a rock fall analysis has been performed and a reasonable estimate of the final location of fallen rocks can be obtained, ditches can be designed to capture errant cobbles and boulders. Guidelines for the dimensioning of capture ditches are provided in FHWA (1998).

Steel face mesh can be installed over rock slope surfaces to restrain material that might otherwise dislodge. The mesh may be relatively fine twisted wire or it may comprise larger diameter elements depending on strength requirements. If the mesh is placed directly on the slope face, it must be secured by anchors that are installed in a regular pattern. In a separate application, the top of the mesh can be secured to a stable section of rock slope and left suspended to drape in front of the slope at lower elevations. Rocks that dislodge from the slope and would otherwise represent a rock fall hazard are intercepted by the mesh curtain. In such applications, a ditch is usually installed below the mesh to capture fallen material. As with reinforcement anchors, steel mesh is subject to corrosion in aggressive electrochemical environments. Both the mesh and its anchor components should be designed with corrosion protection.

Catch fences have become a common feature along highways that pass through mountainous terrain. In general, they are a practical and cost-effective measure to protect against rock falls. However, an assessment of rock fall trajectories is essential to determine both the proper location, height, and structural capacities of such barriers.
key_points: Rock fall protection options include surface mesh, capture ditches, and catch fences.
The design of any rock fall protection measure usually requires an assessment of the risk posed by rock falls; rock fall analyses are generally beyond the capabilities of hand calculations.
When FHWA (1998) was published, computer analysis of rock falls was at a relatively early stage and had to be paired with videography and surveying to give solutions with meaningful accuracy.
Steel face mesh can be anchored directly to the slope face or draped from a stable upper anchor point; a catch ditch below intercepts fallen material.
Catch fences are practical and cost-effective for highway rock fall protection; proper location, height, and capacity depend on trajectory analysis.
Steel mesh and anchors are subject to corrosion in aggressive electrochemical environments and require corrosion protection.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing rock fall protection measures such as mesh, ditches, or catch fences for slopes threatening roads or infrastructure.

sections.title: Rock Sheds and Tunnels
sections.summary: Describes rock sheds, an effective method of protecting vehicular traffic from rock falls whose use is rarely justified unless the cost of other mitigation measures is especially high; typically needed on roadways cut into hillsides, with a roof sloping downhill on beams secured to benches uphill and supported by columns downhill. Where a rock shed is not practical, a tunnel may be necessary (FHWA 1998 describes a railway example in Canada).
sections.body:
Rock sheds are an effective method of protecting vehicular traffic from rock falls, but their use is rarely justified unless the cost of other mitigation measures is especially high. They are typically needed on roadways that have been cut into hillsides. They are designed with a roof that slopes downhill. On the uphill side of the roof, the roof support beams are secured onto benches. On the downhill side of the roof, the roof support beams can be supported by columns.

In locations where it is not practical to construct a rock shed it may be necessary to construct a tunnel. FHWA (1998) describe such an example for a railway in Canada.
key_points: Rock sheds protect vehicular traffic from rock falls but are rarely cost-justified unless other measures are too expensive.
Rock shed roofs slope downhill; uphill beams are bench-supported and downhill beams are column-supported.
In locations where it is not practical to construct a rock shed it may be necessary to construct a tunnel.
FHWA (1998) provides a Canadian railway tunnel example for reference.
sections.applicability: Applies when protecting traffic on roadways cut into hillsides from rock falls where the cost of other mitigation measures is especially high.

key_points: Defines safety factor variants: F (general), Fm (Bishop's Simplified), FR (geosynthetic strength), FW (wedge failure).

Geosynthetic-specific symbols include Tal (long-term tensile strength), TULT (ultimate tensile strength based on MARV), Pr (pullout resistance), Le (embedment length), and reduction factors RFCR, RFD, RFID.
Rock block mechanics symbols: FN (force perpendicular to sliding plane), FS (force parallel to sliding plane), W (block weight), U (uplift force), V (tension crack water force).
Pore pressure represented by both u (pore water pressure) and ru (pore pressure coefficient); seepage captured by S (seepage force) and i (hydraulic gradient).
Greek symbols cover stress state (σ, σʹ, σʹv, τ), friction angles (φ, φʹ, φʹr), unit weights (γ, γw), and wedge/dip geometry (Ψ, ΨFi, Ψi, ΨP, αi).
Symbol α is used for two distinct quantities: dip direction/azimuth and scale correction factor for nonlinear stress reduction.
MARV (Minimum Average Roll Value) is defined here as it underpins the TULT geosynthetic strength parameter.
